title: Module 11 — Procedural Guidance
text:
What clinical question does this exam answer, and how do findings change management?






Note



The bedside decision frame: One overarching principle.
Is this procedure safe to perform here, and how do I do it with the least risk to this patient?
Ultrasound guidance reduces complication rates for all four procedures covered in this module. For central venous access, real-time ultrasound has replaced landmark technique as the standard of care. For thoracentesis, paracentesis, and pericardiocentesis, ultrasound identifies the target, defines the safe approach, and allows real-time confirmation of needle position.


Procedural ultrasound has two phases: 1. Pre-procedural assessment: Is there fluid? How much? What is the best site? What structures must be avoided? 2. Real-time guidance: Watch the needle enter the target in real time.
Both phases reduce risk. Pre-procedural assessment alone (static marking) is better than no ultrasound. Real-time guidance is better still, and is standard for central venous access.

title: Module 11 — Procedural Guidance
text:
2. Central venous access

Clinical rationale
Central venous catheter (CVC) placement under real-time ultrasound guidance reduces arterial puncture, pneumothorax, and number of attempts compared to landmark technique. The NICE guideline (2002) and AHRQ both recommend ultrasound guidance for internal jugular CVC placement as standard of care. Evidence supports its use for subclavian and femoral access as well.



Internal jugular vein






Tip



Video slots: - IJ vein anatomy in transverse — IJ lateral to carotid, compressibility test - Short-axis (out-of-plane) needle guidance — needle tip visualization - Long-axis (in-plane) needle guidance — full needle shaft visualization - Wire confirmation — J-wire in the IJ lumen before dilation


Probe: High-frequency linear (7–15 MHz). Vascular preset.
Anatomy: The IJ vein is anterior and lateral to the carotid artery at the level of the cricoid cartilage. The vein is larger, compressible, and non-pulsatile. The carotid is round, pulsatile, and does not compress.
Approach — short-axis (transverse, out-of-plane): Place the probe in transverse over the IJ vein. Center the vein in the image. Insert the needle at the midpoint of the probe at a 45° angle. The needle appears as a bright dot (hyperechoic) as it enters the image plane. Fan the probe toward the needle tip to track it. Advance into the vein when the tip is visualized in the lumen.
Approach — long-axis (longitudinal, in-plane): Rotate the probe 90° to image the vein in long axis. Insert the needle at the proximal end of the probe, bevel up, at a shallower angle. The entire needle shaft and tip are visible throughout the approach. This approach requires more practice but provides better visualization of needle tip position.
Key steps: 1. Identify the IJ and carotid in transverse — confirm IJ is lateral to carotid. 2. Test compressibility — confirm IJ collapses (not the carotid). 3. Apply color Doppler to confirm venous (non-pulsatile) vs arterial (pulsatile) flow. 4. Guide needle in real-time into the IJ lumen. 5. Confirm venous blood return — dark, non-pulsatile. 6. Advance the J-wire and confirm wire position in the IJ lumen under ultrasound before removing the needle. 7. Confirm wire not in carotid — vein is lateral, compressible, wire appears as a bright line in the lumen.
Teaching points:

The most important step is wire confirmation before dilation. Dilating an arterial access is the catastrophic complication. Ultrasound-confirm the wire is in the correct vessel before proceeding.
Carotid puncture with a dilator or large-bore catheter requires vascular surgery — do not simply remove the catheter from a carotid.
Trendelenburg position distends the IJ (increases venous pressure, enlarges the target).
Right IJ is preferred (straight path to the SVC, avoids thoracic duct on the left, lower pneumothorax risk than subclavian).




Subclavian / infraclavicular approach






Tip



Video slot: Infraclavicular approach — axillary/subclavian vein in long axis, in-plane needle guidance.


Probe: Linear, placed in the infraclavicular fossa, parallel to the clavicle, to image the axillary/subclavian vein in long axis.
Approach: In-plane (long-axis) guidance is preferred for the subclavian approach — this allows visualization of the entire needle shaft as it approaches the vein from lateral to medial. The pleura is visible deep to the vein — keeping the needle superficial to the pleura avoids pneumothorax.
Teaching points:

The subclavian approach is preferred when a lower infection risk is required (long-term catheters, high VAP risk), or when the IJ is inaccessible.
The in-plane long-axis approach dramatically reduces pneumothorax compared to the blind landmark technique.
The subclavian vein is not compressible (it is bounded by the clavicle) — use color Doppler to confirm venous flow.




Femoral vein






Tip



Video slot: Femoral vein access — transverse anatomy at the femoral triangle, compressibility, short-axis guidance.


Probe: Linear, transverse at the femoral triangle. The femoral vein is medial to the femoral artery.
Teaching points:

Femoral access carries the highest infection rate of the three sites — reserve for emergencies or when other sites are not accessible.
Confirm the vein (medial, compressible, non-pulsatile) before advancing. The femoral nerve is lateral to the artery — avoid lateral needle angulation.
Femoral access below the inguinal ligament reduces retroperitoneal hemorrhage risk from inadvertent arterial puncture.

title: Module 11 — Procedural Guidance
text:
3. Thoracentesis

Clinical rationale
Ultrasound-guided thoracentesis reduces the risk of pneumothorax, reduces the rate of dry taps (incorrect site selection), and is now recommended over landmark-based technique for all thoracenteses in the ICU and non-ICU setting.



Pre-procedural assessment






Tip



Video slots: - Effusion assessment — depth, character, loculation - Site marking — selecting the optimal entry point - Safe triangle anatomy


Probe: Curvilinear or phased array, low frequency (2–5 MHz) for depth. Linear for near-field detail.
Pre-procedural checklist: 1. Confirm the effusion is free-flowing — place the patient upright or in lateral decubitus and reassess. A free-flowing effusion layers dependently. A loculated effusion does not shift. 2. Measure the depth — the distance from skin to effusion, and effusion depth at the selected entry site. 3. Identify the diaphragm — confirm the effusion is above the diaphragm (not subphrenic ascites). 4. Look for underlying lung — atelectatic lung floating in the effusion should be identified before needle insertion. 5. Mark the site — apply firm pressure with a marker or a pen cap at the chosen entry point. Mark the depth on the skin.
Safe site selection: - At least one intercostal space below the superior margin of the effusion. - Superior to the lower rib at the chosen interspace — neurovascular bundle runs below the rib. - Lateral enough to avoid the liver (right side) or spleen (left side), but medial to avoid the long thoracic nerve. - Safe triangle: bounded by the anterior border of the latissimus dorsi, the lateral edge of the pectoralis major, and above the 5th intercostal space — the preferred region for lateral decubitus thoracentesis.



Real-time guidance






Tip



Video slot: Real-time thoracentesis — probe in sterile sleeve, needle insertion under direct vision, aspiration confirmed.


Technique: - Sterile probe cover and gel. - Insert needle superior to the rib at the marked interspace, bevel up. - Visualize the needle tip entering the effusion — it appears as a bright hyperechoic dot in the anechoic fluid. - Aspirate — fluid return confirms intrapleural position. - For large-volume drainage, a catheter-over-needle (pigtail catheter) system is preferred.
Post-procedure: - Post-procedure lung ultrasound to assess for pneumothorax (lung sliding should be present). - Re-expansion pulmonary edema risk: limit drainage to 1.5 L per session or stop earlier if the patient develops cough or chest tightness.
Teaching points:

The neurovascular bundle runs in the inferior groove of the rib — always enter superior to the rib.
In a mechanically ventilated patient, thoracentesis can be performed safely with ultrasound guidance. The pneumothorax rate is not higher than in spontaneously breathing patients when ultrasound is used.
If fluid is echogenic (exudate, hemothorax, empyema), a larger-bore chest tube is more appropriate than a needle or small catheter.

title: Module 11 — Procedural Guidance
text:
4. Paracentesis

Clinical rationale
Ultrasound guidance for paracentesis reduces the rate of failed procedures (dry taps) and reduces the risk of bowel perforation, hematoma, and bladder injury. Real-time guidance is preferred over static site marking.



Pre-procedural assessment






Tip



Video slot: Ascites assessment — free fluid location, depth, bowel loops, epigastric vessels.


Probe: Curvilinear, 2–5 MHz.
Pre-procedural checklist: 1. Confirm free fluid — identify a pocket of ascites without bowel loops or adhesions in the needle path. 2. Measure depth — skin-to-fluid distance and fluid pocket depth. 3. Identify the inferior epigastric vessels — using color Doppler, identify the inferior epigastric artery and vein in the lateral abdominal wall. These run between the rectus abdominis and posterior rectus sheath. Puncture lateral to the rectus sheath avoids these vessels. 4. Identify bowel — confirm no bowel loops in the needle path. Bowel is peristaltic, has wall layers, and may contain echogenic contents. 5. Confirm bladder is empty — especially for low midline approaches. Catheterize if necessary.
Site selection: - Left lower quadrant: Most common site — fewer adhesions than the right (no prior appendectomy site), largest fluid pocket in most patients. 2–3 cm medial and 2–3 cm superior to the left anterior superior iliac spine. - Midline: Infraumbilical, in the avascular linea alba. Useful when lateral ascites is minimal. Avoid if previous midline surgery is present (adhesions risk). - Avoid the right lower quadrant (caecum, appendectomy adhesions) and the flanks (inferior epigastric vessels).



Real-time guidance






Tip



Video slot: Real-time paracentesis — probe in sterile sleeve, needle tip in fluid, “Z-track” technique.


Technique: - Sterile probe cover and gel. - Z-track technique: while inserting the needle, apply traction to the skin laterally or superiorly, then release after needle insertion. This displaces the skin puncture site from the muscle/peritoneal puncture site, reducing the risk of persistent ascites leak. - Visualize the needle tip entering the ascites pocket in real time. - Aspirate to confirm fluid return. - Large-volume paracentesis (>5 L): replace 8 g albumin per liter removed to prevent paracentesis-induced circulatory dysfunction.
Teaching points:

Coagulopathy is not a contraindication to ultrasound-guided paracentesis in most patients — the complication rate is low even in patients with elevated INR and low platelets. Routine FFP or platelet transfusion pre-paracentesis is not supported by evidence.
Send fluid for cell count, total protein, albumin (to calculate SAAG), culture, and cytology as indicated.
Bloody fluid on aspiration: check if it clears (traumatic tap) or remains bloody (hemoperitoneum). A hematocrit on the fluid compared to serum hematocrit helps distinguish.

title: Module 11 — Procedural Guidance
text:
5. Pericardiocentesis

Clinical rationale
Ultrasound guidance for pericardiocentesis identifies the largest accessible fluid pocket, guides needle direction, confirms needle position in the pericardial space, and reduces the risk of cardiac puncture and pneumothorax. All elective pericardiocenteses should be performed under ultrasound guidance. In extremis, the subxiphoid blind approach remains an option, but ultrasound should be used whenever possible.



Pre-procedural assessment






Tip



Video slot: Pre-procedure pericardiocentesis assessment — largest pocket, optimal window, effusion depth.


Probe: Phased array, cardiac preset.
Pre-procedural checklist: 1. Confirm the effusion — in at least two windows (subcostal, PLAX, apical). 2. Identify the largest, most accessible pocket — the needle must travel the shortest distance to reach the most fluid. 3. Measure the depth — skin-to-pericardium distance at the planned entry site. 4. Identify the path — confirm no liver, lung, or bowel in the needle trajectory. 5. Assess for tamponade physiology — confirms urgency.
Common approaches:








Approach
Best For
Avoid If




Subxiphoid
Large posterior/inferior effusions, emergency
Liver in the path, prior abdominal surgery


Apical
Large lateral/apical effusions
Lung in the path, small effusion


Parasternal
Anterior effusions
Not preferred (coronary vessels nearby)






Real-time guidance






Tip



Video slot: Real-time pericardiocentesis — needle tip entering the pericardial space, agitated saline confirmation, catheter in the pericardial space.


Technique: - Sterile probe cover and gel. - Insert the needle under continuous real-time visualization. The needle appears as a bright hyperechoic line entering the pericardial fluid. - Agitated saline (bubble study): Once fluid is aspirated, inject 5–10 mL of agitated saline (mixed with a small amount of air). If the bubbles appear in the pericardial space (surrounding the heart), the needle is correctly positioned. If bubbles appear inside a cardiac chamber, the needle has entered the heart — withdraw immediately. - Place a guidewire and dilate over the wire to insert a pigtail drainage catheter for ongoing drainage. - Confirm catheter position with echo — the pigtail tip should be visible in the pericardial space.
Post-procedure: - Repeat echo after drainage to confirm reduction in effusion and resolution of tamponade physiology. - Leave the catheter in place until drainage is <25–50 mL per day for recurrent or malignant effusions. - Send fluid for cell count, LDH, protein, glucose, culture (bacterial, fungal, TB), cytology, and hematocrit.
Teaching points:

If the needle hits the heart (epicardial contact), the catheter tip will deflect or “dance” with each heartbeat. Withdraw slightly.
Blood aspirated from the pericardial space does not clot (it has been defibrinated by cardiac motion). Blood from a cardiac chamber clots. This helps distinguish pericardial hemorrhage from inadvertent cardiac puncture.
In extremis (patient pulseless or prearrest), the blind subxiphoid approach is acceptable — angle the needle toward the left shoulder at 30–45° from horizontal, advance while aspirating.
Coagulopathy significantly increases the risk of pericardiocentesis — correct coagulopathy before elective drainage when possible.

title: Module 11 — Procedural Guidance
text:
6. Integration cases
Cases where procedural ultrasound changes management.


Case 1: Difficult IJ — obesity and short neck
Clinical scenario: A 130 kg man with a BMI of 46 and a short neck requires a central venous catheter for vasopressor administration. The team is debating femoral access due to concern about the neck anatomy.
What you do: Bedside assessment of the IJ with a linear probe before selecting the site.






Tip



Video slot: Loops for assessment.


What you see: Right IJ: large, easily visualized, lateral to the carotid, fully compressible. Depth 2.1 cm. No anomalous anatomy.
How does this change management? The IJ is accessible and low-risk under real-time ultrasound guidance despite the body habitus. Proceed with right IJ CVC using real-time in-plane (long-axis) guidance. Avoid femoral access (higher infection risk) when IJ is accessible. Ultrasound-based assessment has prevented an unnecessary decision to use a higher-risk site based on external appearance alone.



Case 2: Thoracentesis in a ventilated patient
Clinical scenario: A 62-year-old woman on day 7 of mechanical ventilation for ARDS has a large right pleural effusion visible on CXR, contributing to difficult oxygenation. The team wants to drain it but is concerned about pneumothorax risk in a ventilated patient.
What you do: Pre-procedural ultrasound assessment of the right pleural effusion.






Tip



Video slot: Loops for assessment.


What you see: Large, free-flowing right pleural effusion. Maximum effusion depth 7 cm at the PLAPS point. No loculation. Diaphragm clearly identified. Atelectatic lung floating in the effusion. Depth from skin to fluid: 2.3 cm.
How does this change management? Proceed with real-time ultrasound-guided thoracentesis in the lateral decubitus position (if tolerated) or seated position. The pneumothorax rate with ultrasound guidance in ventilated patients is not higher than in spontaneously breathing patients. Mark the entry site, use real-time guidance, and monitor with post-procedure lung ultrasound (restored lung sliding confirms no pneumothorax). This patient’s oxygenation should improve significantly after drainage.



Case 3: Pericardiocentesis — where is the largest pocket?
Clinical scenario: A 58-year-old man with malignant pericardial effusion and tamponade physiology requires urgent pericardiocentesis. The cardiology fellow asks which approach to use.
What you do: Pre-procedural echo to assess all windows and identify the optimal approach.






Tip



Video slot: Loops for assessment.


What you see: Subcostal: large effusion, liver in the subxiphoid needle path. Apical: large effusion anterior and lateral to the apex, 2.5 cm depth from the skin. PLAX: effusion posterior and anterior, 3.0 cm posterior.
How does this change management? The liver obstructs the subxiphoid approach. The apical approach has the shortest path to the largest accessible pocket and no intervening structures in the trajectory. Proceed with apical pericardiocentesis under real-time ultrasound guidance. This pre-procedural assessment has changed the approach and likely prevented a hepatic puncture.






Tip



Procedural principle: Pre-procedural assessment is not optional. The anatomy you assume is not the anatomy that exists.

title: Module 11 — Procedural Guidance
text:
Quiz
Anki deck for spaced repetition: link coming soon.






Note



Q1. You insert a wire for a right IJ CVC. Before dilating, how do you confirm the wire is in the vein and not the carotid artery?






Caution





Answer Confirm wire position under real-time ultrasound. Visualize the wire (bright hyperechoic line) in the IJ lumen on transverse view — the IJ is lateral and compressible, the carotid is medial and pulsatile. If wire location is uncertain, use color Doppler to distinguish venous from arterial flow. Alternatively, transduce the catheter before dilation (venous waveform vs arterial waveform). Never dilate before confirming venous position — dilating a carotid arteriotomy requires vascular surgery.



Q2. During thoracentesis, the patient coughs and the needle contacts the lower rib. What do you do?






Caution





Answer Stop and withdraw the needle — do not advance when the needle has shifted off the intended trajectory. Rib contact risks laceration of the intercostal neurovascular bundle (inferior groove of the rib). Reassess under ultrasound, reconfirm the effusion and the safe window, and re-enter superior to the rib at the chosen interspace. The neurovascular bundle runs in a groove on the inferior aspect of each rib — always enter superior to the lower rib.



Q3. You aspirate blood during pericardiocentesis. How do you determine whether the blood is from the pericardial space or from inadvertent cardiac puncture?






Caution





Answer Two methods: (1) Inject agitated saline — if bubbles appear in the pericardial space (visible as echogenic material surrounding the heart), the needle is correctly positioned; if bubbles appear inside a cardiac chamber, the needle is in the heart. (2) Pericardial blood does not clot (it is defibrinated by cardiac motion), while intracardiac blood clots rapidly. Also: if the catheter tip is visible “dancing” with each heartbeat, it is likely against the myocardium — withdraw slightly.



Q4. Why is the Z-track technique used during paracentesis, and what does it accomplish?






Caution





Answer The Z-track technique creates a non-linear path between the skin puncture and the peritoneal puncture — the skin is retracted laterally or superiorly before needle insertion and released afterward. When released, the skin returns to its original position, creating a tortuous path that resists ascitic fluid from leaking out along the needle track after catheter removal. This reduces the incidence of persistent ascitic leak through the puncture site.



Q5. What is the most common complication of ultrasound-guided central venous access, and how does real-time guidance reduce it?






Caution





Answer Arterial puncture (carotid for IJ access) is the most common and most serious acute complication. Real-time ultrasound guidance reduces arterial puncture by allowing direct visualization of the needle tip entering the venous lumen rather than relying on landmark estimation. The vein is identified, compressibility is confirmed, and the needle is watched in real-time as it enters the lumen — dramatically reducing inadvertent arterial access compared to the landmark technique.

title: Module 9 — Abdominal Ultrasound
text:
What clinical question does this exam answer, and how do findings change management?






Note



The bedside decision frame: Four distinct questions, each with its own clinical trigger.

Is there intraperitoneal free fluid? In trauma, free fluid = blood until proven otherwise. In the non-trauma ICU patient, free fluid may represent ascites, hollow viscus perforation, or internal hemorrhage.
Is there a distended, obstructed bladder? Urinary retention is a common, painful, and easily treated problem — one that is frequently missed in sedated or altered patients.
Is there hydronephrosis? Ureteral obstruction causing hydronephrosis may explain AKI, flank pain, or urosepsis in an undrained system.
In the trauma patient — is there free fluid in the pericardium? The subxiphoid FAST view incorporates cardiac assessment (see Module 1).



Abdominal ultrasound at the bedside is fast, non-invasive, and immediately actionable. The FAST exam (Focused Assessment with Sonography in Trauma) is the standard of care in trauma resuscitation. In non-trauma critical care, bladder and kidney assessment are high-yield applications that require minimal additional training.

title: Module 9 — Abdominal Ultrasound
text:
2. Image acquisition
Probe, windows, and technique for this module.
Use a curvilinear (low-frequency, 2–5 MHz) probe for all abdominal windows — the penetration depth required for the liver, spleen, kidneys, and pelvis exceeds what a linear probe provides. A phased array probe is an acceptable substitute for FAST but is less ideal for the pelvic view.
Machine preset: Abdominal. Adjust depth to see structures of interest with adequate margin.


Right upper quadrant — Morrison’s pouch






Tip



Video slot: RUQ acquisition — hepatorenal interface, fan through Morrison’s pouch, assess for free fluid.


Probe placement: Probe in the right mid-axillary line, 8th–11th intercostal space, indicator toward the patient’s head. Fan through the hepatorenal interface (Morrison’s pouch) — the potential space between the liver and right kidney.
What you are looking for: Any anechoic (black) stripe between the liver and right kidney. In a normal exam, the liver and kidney appear to be in direct contact with a thin hyperechoic stripe of Gerota’s fascia between them. Free fluid appears as a wedge or stripe of anechoic material in the dependent hepatorenal space. Also assess the inferior tip of the liver and the right paracolic gutter.
Pearls: Morrison’s pouch is the most dependent intraperitoneal space in the supine position and the most sensitive location for detecting free fluid. As little as 100–200 mL of free fluid may be visible here.



Left upper quadrant — splenorenal space






Tip



Video slot: LUQ acquisition — splenorenal interface, subphrenic space, left paracolic gutter.


Probe placement: Left posterior axillary line, 8th–11th intercostal space, indicator toward the head. This window is more posterior than the RUQ view — a common error is imaging too anteriorly and missing the spleen.
What you are looking for: Free fluid between the spleen and left kidney (splenorenal space), and in the subphrenic space (between the diaphragm and spleen). A left pleural effusion appears above the diaphragm — do not confuse it with subphrenic free fluid. The diaphragm is the landmark: fluid above = pleural, fluid below = peritoneal.
Pearls: The LUQ is less sensitive than the RUQ because the splenorenal space is less dependent. Free fluid may not accumulate here until larger volumes are present. Assess the subphrenic and paracolic regions thoroughly.



Suprapubic — pelvis






Tip



Video slot: Suprapubic acquisition — bladder as acoustic window, free fluid in the pouch of Douglas (female) or rectovesical space (male), transverse and sagittal planes.


Probe placement: Suprapubic, just above the symphysis pubis, indicator to the patient’s right (transverse) or head (sagittal). The bladder serves as an acoustic window to the posterior pelvic structures.
What you are looking for: Free fluid posterior to the bladder (pouch of Douglas in females, rectovesical space in males). In females, look for fluid in the cul-de-sac posterior to the uterus. Scan in both transverse and sagittal planes. Free fluid appears anechoic, dependent, and irregular in shape.
Bladder assessment: See dedicated section below.
Pearls: The pelvic view requires a full or at least partially full bladder to serve as an acoustic window. In patients who are oliguric or have been catheterized, the pelvic view may be limited. The pelvic space is the most dependent location in the erect position — significant fluid may accumulate here even when the upper quadrants appear negative.



Subxiphoid — pericardium and cardiac
Covered in Module 1. The subxiphoid view is the fourth standard FAST window.



Bladder — transverse and sagittal






Tip



Video slot: Bladder assessment — full bladder as an anechoic structure, volume estimation, wall assessment.


Probe placement: Suprapubic, transverse then sagittal. The bladder appears as a well-defined anechoic structure posterior to the symphysis. Measure three dimensions: transverse (width), anteroposterior (depth), and craniocaudal (height). Bladder volume (mL) ≈ 0.52 × width × depth × height (in cm). Some machines calculate this automatically.
Significant residual volume: >300 mL post-void, or a distended bladder in a patient with reduced consciousness who is not catheterized.



Kidneys — longitudinal






Tip



Video slot: Right and left kidney — normal cortex and collecting system vs hydronephrosis grades.


Probe placement: Coronal plane, similar to FAST views but oriented to the kidneys. Right kidney: right mid-axillary line, indicator up. Left kidney: left posterior axillary line, indicator up. Obtain a longitudinal image of the entire kidney — cortex, medullary pyramids, and collecting system (renal pelvis and calyces).
What you are looking for: Any separation of the renal sinus (echogenic central collecting system) by anechoic fluid — indicating hydronephrosis.

title: Module 9 — Abdominal Ultrasound
text:
3. Normal & normal variants






Tip



Video slots: Normal FAST exam — no free fluid at each window. Normal kidney. Normal bladder.



Normal FAST exam
No anechoic fluid in Morrison’s pouch, splenorenal space, or pelvis. The subxiphoid view shows no pericardial effusion. Organ surfaces are in direct contact with each other and with the abdominal wall.


Normal kidney
Length 9–12 cm, width 4–6 cm. The renal cortex is slightly less echogenic than the liver. The renal sinus (collecting system) appears as a central echogenic structure without internal fluid. Medullary pyramids appear as hypoechoic triangular structures pointing toward the sinus.


Normal bladder
Thin-walled, smooth, anechoic. Wall thickness <3 mm when full. Urine is anechoic; debris, clots, or calculi appear as echogenic foci within the lumen.


Perihepatic fat and ascites mimics
Small amounts of fat around the liver and mesentery can mimic minimal free fluid. Fat has a characteristic echogenicity (not purely anechoic) and does not layer into dependent spaces the way free fluid does. Bowel loops with fluid should not be mistaken for free fluid — identify peristalsis and bowel wall to distinguish.

title: Module 9 — Abdominal Ultrasound
text:
4. Pathology library
Organized by finding.

Free fluid — traumatic (hemoperitoneum)






Tip



Video slots: - Anechoic free fluid in Morrison’s pouch - Moderate-large free fluid in the pelvis - Echogenic free fluid — acute blood


In trauma, any free fluid is assumed to be blood. Acute hemoperitoneum may be anechoic (early, not clotted) or echogenic (clotted blood). The pattern and volume guide management.
Grading by volume and distribution:








Finding
Estimated Volume
Management Implication




Trace fluid in Morrison’s pouch only
<250 mL
Serial exam, reassess


Fluid in RUQ + pelvis
500–1000 mL
Operative vs non-operative decision based on hemodynamics


Fluid in all three windows
>1000 mL
Likely operative in hemodynamically unstable patient



Teaching points:

A positive FAST in a hemodynamically unstable patient = OR, not CT. Do not delay operative intervention for imaging.
A negative FAST does not rule out intraperitoneal injury — solid organ injuries may be present without free fluid early.
A positive FAST in a hemodynamically stable patient allows CT for better injury characterization before operative decision.
Echogenic (bright) free fluid = acute blood/clot. Anechoic free fluid in trauma = blood (until proven otherwise), even if it looks like simple fluid.




Free fluid — non-traumatic






Tip



Video slot: Ascites — large volume anechoic free fluid surrounding bowel loops, “floating” bowel.


In the non-trauma ICU patient, free fluid may represent: - Ascites: Cirrhosis, malignancy, heart failure — anechoic, often massive, bowel loops appear to float - Ruptured viscus: Bowel perforation — complex, echogenic, or mixed fluid - Ruptured ectopic pregnancy: Pelvic free fluid in a woman of childbearing age = ectopic until proven otherwise - Internal hemorrhage: Post-procedural, anticoagulated, aortic aneurysm rupture
Teaching points:

In a non-trauma patient with hypotension and pelvic free fluid, always check a urine or serum beta-hCG before attributing fluid to another cause.
Ruptured ectopic with free fluid and hemodynamic instability = emergent gynecologic surgery.
Large ascites can be drained under ultrasound guidance (see Module 11).




Urinary retention and bladder assessment






Tip



Video slots: - Massively distended bladder — large anechoic structure filling the pelvis - Bladder volume calculation with three-plane measurement


A distended bladder (>300 mL post-void residual) in a patient with reduced consciousness, confusion, agitation, or unexplained pain is urinary retention until proven otherwise.
Teaching points:

Urinary retention is common in the ICU — opioids, anticholinergics, and sedatives all reduce detrusor function.
In a male patient with an enlarged prostate, any acute illness may precipitate retention.
A fully distended bladder (>500–800 mL) can reflexively inhibit cardiac output and worsen hemodynamics.
Treatment is urethral or suprapubic catheterization. Ultrasound-guided suprapubic catheterization is appropriate when urethral access is not possible.
Post-decompression diuresis can occur after relief of chronic obstruction — anticipate and replace fluids.




Hydronephrosis






Tip



Video slots: - Grade 1 hydronephrosis — mild dilation of the renal pelvis only - Grade 2 — dilation of pelvis and calyces, preserved cortex - Grade 3 — severe dilation, thinned cortex


Hydronephrosis is dilation of the renal collecting system from ureteral obstruction. It appears as anechoic fluid within the renal sinus, separating the echogenic collecting system walls.
Grading:



Grade
Appearance




1 (mild)
Pelvis dilated, calyces normal


2 (moderate)
Pelvis and calyces dilated, cortex preserved


3 (severe)
Marked dilation, cortex thinned



Teaching points:

Hydronephrosis in a patient with AKI = obstructive nephropathy until proven otherwise. Relieve the obstruction (Foley, ureteral stent, nephrostomy) before attributing the AKI to another cause.
Bilateral hydronephrosis = bilateral obstruction or bladder outlet obstruction (BPH, mass). Check the bladder first.
Hydronephrosis + fever = obstructed, infected system (pyonephrosis) — urgent drainage is required (not just antibiotics).
Normal ultrasound does not rule out obstruction in early or acute cases — the collecting system may not have had time to dilate.

title: Module 9 — Abdominal Ultrasound
text:
5. Integration cases
Cases where the finding changes management.


Case 1: Trauma — positive FAST in a hypotensive patient
Clinical scenario: A 25-year-old man is brought in after a motor vehicle collision at highway speed. He is hypotensive (BP 78/50) and tachycardic (HR 132) on arrival. GCS is 14. The trauma team is assembled.
What exam would you perform? Immediate FAST exam as part of the primary survey.






Tip



Video slot: Loops for interpretation.


What you see: Morrison’s pouch: free fluid, moderate volume. Splenorenal space: free fluid. Pelvis: large volume free fluid. Subxiphoid: no pericardial effusion.
How does this change management? Positive FAST with hemodynamic instability = operative intervention. Do not take this patient to CT. Transfuse blood products in a 1:1:1 ratio (PRBC:FFP:platelets) as a bridge to the OR. Activate massive transfusion protocol. The trauma surgeon takes over — the bedside echo has already answered the most important question.



Case 2: Urosepsis with flank pain — is the system obstructed?
Clinical scenario: A 70-year-old man with a history of kidney stones presents with fever (39.2°C), right flank pain, and hypotension. UA shows pyuria. He is started on IV antibiotics and fluids. The team is wondering if he needs urgent urologic intervention.
What exam would you perform? Renal ultrasound — bilateral kidneys.






Tip



Video slot: Loops for interpretation.


What you see: Right kidney: grade 2–3 hydronephrosis. Echogenic material within the dilated collecting system (debris). Left kidney: normal.
How does this change management? Obstructed, infected right kidney — pyonephrosis. Antibiotics alone are insufficient. Emergent urology consultation for urgent drainage — either ureteral stent or percutaneous nephrostomy. Septic shock from an obstructed system will not resolve without drainage. This is a surgical emergency, not a medical one.



Case 3: Altered mental status and agitation — is this retention?
Clinical scenario: A 77-year-old man with BPH, on post-op day 1 following a hip replacement, is increasingly agitated and confused. Vitals are stable. He received significant opioids intraoperatively. His Foley was removed 4 hours ago.
What exam would you perform? Bladder ultrasound.






Tip



Video slot: Loops for interpretation.


What you see: Distended, smooth-walled bladder. Estimated volume 680 mL.
How does this change management? Urinary retention causing agitation and delirium in a post-operative elderly male. Replace the urethral catheter. Agitation should resolve within minutes of bladder decompression. Avoid sedatives — they will worsen delirium without treating the cause. Monitor for post-obstructive diuresis. Address BPH pharmacologically (alpha-blocker) before the next void trial.



Case 4: Ruptured ectopic pregnancy
Clinical scenario: A 28-year-old woman presents to the ED with sudden-onset lower abdominal pain and presyncope. BP 90/60, HR 118. She reports her last menstrual period was 7 weeks ago. She thought she might be pregnant but has not confirmed it.
What exam would you perform? FAST exam with attention to the pelvic view, and immediate beta-hCG.






Tip



Video slot: Loops for interpretation.


What you see: Large volume of free fluid in the pelvis and RUQ. No intrauterine pregnancy visible. Echogenic mass adjacent to the left ovary. Beta-hCG returns at 4,200 mIU/mL.
How does this change management? Ruptured ectopic pregnancy with hemoperitoneum. This is a surgical emergency. Call OB/GYN for emergent surgical intervention. Two large-bore IVs, blood type and crossmatch, activate the OR. Do not perform a diagnostic laparoscopy — this patient needs a therapeutic laparotomy or laparoscopy. Time is critical.






Tip

title: Module 9 — Abdominal Ultrasound
text:
Quiz
Anki deck for spaced repetition: link coming soon.






Note



Q1. Where is the most sensitive location for detecting free fluid in a supine patient, and why?






Caution





Answer Morrison’s pouch (the hepatorenal space in the right upper quadrant) is the most sensitive location because it is the most dependent intraperitoneal space in the supine patient. Fluid accumulates there preferentially due to gravity. As little as 100–200 mL of free fluid may be visible at this location before it is detectable elsewhere.



Q2. A FAST exam is negative in a hemodynamically stable trauma patient with abdominal tenderness. What is the next step?






Caution





Answer A negative FAST does not rule out solid organ injury or retroperitoneal injury. In a stable patient with abdominal tenderness and a mechanism concerning for injury, CT of the abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast is the next step. CT has much higher sensitivity than ultrasound for detecting solid organ lacerations that have not yet bled into the peritoneum.



Q3. You detect hydronephrosis in a patient with new AKI. What is the next clinical question?






Caution





Answer Is the obstruction bilateral or unilateral? Bilateral hydronephrosis (or hydronephrosis in a solitary kidney) explains AKI — the obstruction must be relieved urgently. Unilateral hydronephrosis alone does not explain AKI unless the contralateral kidney is absent or non-functional. Also ask: is there fever or signs of infection? If so, the obstructed system is infected (pyonephrosis) and requires emergent drainage, not just observation.



Q4. A left pleural effusion appears as fluid above the diaphragm on the LUQ view. How do you distinguish it from subphrenic free fluid?






Caution





Answer The diaphragm is the key landmark — it appears as a bright echogenic curved line. Pleural fluid is above the diaphragm (between the lung and the diaphragm). Peritoneal free fluid is below the diaphragm (in the subphrenic or splenorenal space). The “mirror artifact” — a mirror image of the spleen or liver appearing above the diaphragm — is a normal artifact in the absence of pleural fluid. The presence of a true anechoic collection above the diaphragm that does not show the mirror artifact indicates a pleural effusion.



Q5. Why is pelvic free fluid in a woman of reproductive age a critical finding that requires immediate additional testing?






Caution





Answer Pelvic free fluid in a reproductive-age woman must be evaluated for ruptured ectopic pregnancy — a life-threatening condition that can produce rapid exsanguination. A urine or serum beta-hCG must be obtained immediately. If beta-hCG is positive and there is no intrauterine pregnancy on ultrasound, ruptured ectopic is highly likely until proven otherwise. Hemodynamic instability with pelvic free fluid and a positive beta-hCG = emergent surgical intervention, not further imaging.

title: Module 7 — Basic Valve Assessment
text:
What clinical question does this exam answer, and how do findings change management?






Note



The bedside decision frame: One question with two branches.
Is there significant valvular pathology contributing to this patient’s hemodynamic or respiratory presentation?

Stenosis obstructs forward flow — it limits cardiac output and causes pressure overload upstream.
Regurgitation creates a volume leak — it wastes stroke volume and volume-overloads the chamber receiving the regurgitant jet.

The bedside exam does not replace formal echocardiography for grading severity. It answers whether a valve problem is present, whether it is likely to be severe, and whether it changes immediate management.


Valvular pathology is identified at the bedside with 2D assessment of valve morphology and motion, and with color Doppler to detect regurgitant jets. Quantitative Doppler gradients (CW Doppler, pressure half-time) require training beyond the scope of basic critical care echo, but the qualitative findings — dense calcification, restricted opening, a large regurgitant jet — are accessible to any provider who can obtain the standard windows.

text:
2. Image acquisition
Probe, windows, and technique for this module.
Use a phased array (cardiac) probe on the cardiac preset. Color Doppler requires setting a color box over the valve of interest; keep the box small to maintain frame rate. Align the Doppler beam as parallel as possible to the direction of blood flow — jets aimed away from the beam will be underestimated.


Parasternal long axis — aortic and mitral valves






Tip



Video slot: PLAX with color Doppler across the aortic and mitral valves — normal vs pathologic jets.


What you are looking for: - Aortic valve: Three thin leaflets opening widely in systole. Restricted opening, thickening, or calcification suggests stenosis. Color Doppler in systole: no flow acceleration (no aliasing/turbulence) in a normal valve. - Mitral valve: Anterior leaflet swings widely open in diastole (the “fish mouth” opens). Restricted diastolic opening suggests stenosis. Color Doppler in systole: any jet directed back into the LA suggests regurgitation.



Parasternal short axis — aortic valve






Tip



Video slot: PSAX at the aortic valve level — the “Mercedes-Benz” sign of a normal tricuspid valve, the reduced orifice area of severe AS, bicuspid valve appearance.


What you are looking for: Three equal leaflets forming a Y-shaped (Mercedes-Benz) configuration on closure. Bicuspid aortic valve: two leaflets, fish-mouth opening, often with a raphe. Dense calcification and reduced orifice area indicate severe stenosis.



Apical four-chamber — mitral and tricuspid valves






Tip



Video slot: A4C with color Doppler — mitral regurgitation jet into the LA, tricuspid regurgitation jet into the RA.


What you are looking for: - MR jet: color Doppler in systole, jet directed from LV into LA. A jet occupying >50% of the LA area suggests severe MR (qualitative). - TR jet: color Doppler in systole, jet from RV into RA. Large TR jets allow RVSP estimation (4v² + RAP, where v is the peak TR velocity by CW Doppler).



Apical five-chamber or apical long axis — aortic valve






Tip



Video slot: Apical 5-chamber or APLAX with color Doppler across the aortic valve — turbulent systolic jet in AS, diastolic regurgitant jet in AR.



What you are looking for: - AS: color aliasing (turbulent flow) in systole directed from LV through the LVOT and aortic valve into the aorta. - AR: diastolic jet directed from the aortic valve back into the LVOT. Width of the jet relative to the LVOT width correlates with severity.

title: Module 7 — Basic Valve Assessment
text:
3. Normal & normal variants






Tip



Video slots: Normal aortic, mitral, and tricuspid valves — 2D morphology and color Doppler. Normal trace MR and TR as variants.



Normal aortic valve
Three thin, pliable leaflets that open fully (touching the aortic walls) in systole and coapt centrally in diastole. No color aliasing in systole. No diastolic regurgitant jet. Leaflet thickening without calcification or restriction — aortic sclerosis — is common in older adults and does not cause obstruction.


Normal mitral valve
Anterior and posterior leaflets with wide diastolic excursion. The anterior leaflet is larger and dominates the image on PLAX. Normal coaptation in systole with no gap between leaflets. A trace MR jet on color Doppler is a normal variant (present in up to 70% of normal subjects) — it is central, brief, and small.


Normal tricuspid valve
Three leaflets visible on subcostal and apical views. Trace TR is a normal variant and is used to estimate RVSP — a normal RVSP is less than 35 mmHg. Mild TR without RV dilation is not pathologic.


Physiologic regurgitation
Trace MR, trace TR, and trace pulmonary regurgitation are all common normal variants detectable by sensitive color Doppler. They are identified by their small jet area, brief duration, and absence of structural valve abnormality or downstream chamber dilation.

title: Module 7 — Basic Valve Assessment
text:
4. Pathology library
Organized by valve and finding.

Aortic stenosis






Tip



Video slots: - Calcific AS — dense leaflet calcification, reduced opening on PLAX and PSAX - Color Doppler turbulent jet in systole - Severely reduced aortic valve opening area on PSAX


Calcific aortic stenosis is the most common valvular disease in adults over 65. The leaflets are thickened, echogenic, and immobile. The orifice area on PSAX is visually reduced.
Bedside qualitative severity markers:



Finding
Suggests Severe AS




Dense calcification of all leaflets
Yes


Reduced or absent leaflet excursion
Yes


Visually small orifice on PSAX
Yes


Hyperdynamic LV compensating
Chronic, compensated


Reduced LV function
Decompensated, late



Teaching points:

Critical AS in a hypotensive patient is a cardiac surgery emergency — urgent AVR or TAVR is the only definitive treatment.
Avoid vasodilators in severe AS — they drop afterload without increasing cardiac output (the valve is the fixed obstruction) and can cause precipitous hypotension.
Intra-aortic balloon pump can temporize hemodynamics as a bridge.
Low-flow, low-gradient AS (severe stenosis with reduced EF) can be missed on Doppler — the gradient is low because the ventricle cannot generate adequate flow. 2D morphology is critical.




Aortic regurgitation






Tip



Video slots: - Acute AR — diastolic jet, hyperdynamic LV, premature mitral valve closure - Chronic AR — dilated LV with a large AR jet, preserved function


AR causes diastolic backflow from the aorta into the LV. Acute AR (endocarditis, aortic dissection, trauma) is a hemodynamic emergency — the unprepared LV cannot accommodate the sudden volume load.
Key bedside features:

Diastolic color Doppler jet from aortic valve into LVOT (apical 5-chamber or APLAX view)
Acute AR: Hyperdynamic LV (not yet dilated), premature mitral valve closure on M-mode (diastolic pressure rises rapidly, closes the mitral valve before atrial contraction — a sign of severely elevated LVEDP)
Chronic AR: Dilated, volume-overloaded LV with preserved or reduced EF depending on stage

Teaching points:

Acute AR from aortic dissection or endocarditis is a surgical emergency. Do not delay for hemodynamic stabilization — call CT surgery.
Premature mitral valve closure is a critical finding that indicates the LVEDP has exceeded LA pressure — the LV is in crisis.
Vasodilators (nitroprusside) can reduce regurgitant fraction acutely in non-operative candidates; IABP is contraindicated (increases diastolic aortic pressure, worsening regurgitation).




Mitral regurgitation






Tip



Video slots: - Acute MR from flail leaflet — eccentric, wall-hugging jet, hyperdynamic LV - Chronic MR — large central jet, dilated LA, dilated LV - Ischemic MR — inferior wall motion abnormality with posteriorly directed jet


MR causes systolic backflow from the LV into the LA. Acute MR (papillary muscle rupture, chordal rupture, endocarditis) is poorly tolerated — the LA has not had time to dilate and pressures rise acutely.
Key bedside features:

Systolic color jet from LV into LA on A4C or PLAX
Acute MR: Eccentric, wall-hugging jet (Coanda effect — may be underestimated by color Doppler), hyperdynamic LV, non-dilated LA, pulmonary edema out of proportion to LV function
Chronic MR: Large central or posteriorly directed jet, dilated LA, dilated LV
Ischemic MR: Regional wall motion abnormality (usually inferior/posterior), posteriorly directed jet from malcoaptation

Teaching points:

Acute MR from papillary muscle rupture complicating inferior MI is a surgical emergency. The echo finding of a flail posterior leaflet with an inferior RWMA should trigger immediate cardiac surgery consultation.
Eccentric jets in acute MR are frequently underestimated by color Doppler — the jet wraps along the LA wall and appears smaller than it is.
Do not mistake a small eccentric jet for mild MR without examining the LA size and the hemodynamic picture.




Mitral stenosis






Tip



Video slots: - Rheumatic MS — hockey stick anterior leaflet deformity, reduced diastolic separation, commissural fusion - Color Doppler: diastolic turbulence through the mitral valve


MS causes obstruction to diastolic LV filling. Almost always rheumatic in etiology. The anterior mitral leaflet takes on a “hockey stick” or “elbow” deformity — the body of the leaflet bows toward the septum while the restricted tip remains tethered.
Key bedside features:

Restricted mitral valve diastolic opening on PLAX (normal excursion >2.5 cm)
Hockey stick deformity of the anterior leaflet
Commissural fusion on PSAX — the leaflets appear fused at the commissures, with a reduced orifice area
Color Doppler: high-velocity diastolic jet through the MV into the LV
LA dilation (chronic pressure overload)

Teaching points:

MS in a patient with new atrial fibrillation and hemodynamic compromise is an emergency — tachycardia eliminates diastolic filling time and can precipitate flash pulmonary edema. Rate control (not cardioversion as first-line) is the priority.
Balloon mitral valvuloplasty is the intervention of choice for favorable anatomy. Bedside echo helps triage urgency.
In pregnant patients, MS is the valvular lesion most likely to cause acute decompensation.




Tricuspid regurgitation and RVSP estimation






Tip



Video slots: - TR jet on color Doppler — A4C view - CW Doppler through TR jet — peak velocity for RVSP calculation


TR is most often functional (secondary to RV dilation) rather than primary leaflet disease. RVSP estimation from the peak TR velocity is one of the most useful quantitative measurements available at the bedside.
RVSP = 4 × (peak TR velocity)² + estimated RAP
Estimated RAP from IVC (see Module 5): 5 mmHg (small, collapsible), 10 mmHg (intermediate), 15–20 mmHg (large, non-collapsing).
Teaching points:

RVSP >35 mmHg = pulmonary hypertension. RVSP >60 mmHg = severe pulmonary hypertension.
Accurate measurement requires CW Doppler aligned parallel to the TR jet — off-axis measurements underestimate velocity.
Severe TR can reduce the gradient (low peak velocity) even with severe RV failure, because the RA pressure rises to meet the RV pressure.
Flail tricuspid leaflet from pacemaker lead injury, endocarditis, or trauma — large eccentric TR jet, RV dilation, systemic venous congestion.

text:
5. Integration cases
Cases where the finding changes management.


Case 1: Hypotensive patient with critical aortic stenosis
Clinical scenario: A 78-year-old woman with known “moderate” aortic stenosis is admitted with a syncopal episode and is now hypotensive (BP 82/54). She is pale, with a grade 3/6 systolic murmur at the right upper sternal border radiating to the carotids.
What exam would you perform? Focused cardiac ultrasound — aortic valve, LV function.






Tip



Video slot: Loops for interpretation.


What you see: Dense aortic valve calcification. Reduced leaflet excursion. Visually small orifice on PSAX. LV mildly reduced EF (40%). Hyperdynamic response absent.
How does this change management? Critical AS with decompensated LV — this is low-flow, low-gradient severe AS. Avoid vasodilators and aggressive diuretics (she needs preload). Urgent cardiology and CT surgery consultation for TAVR or surgical AVR. The decision about the approach will be made at the valve center, not in the ED — transfer urgently. IABP may be considered as a bridge in refractory hemodynamic compromise.



Case 2: Acute pulmonary edema after inferior MI
Clinical scenario: A 63-year-old man is 48 hours post-inferior STEMI (now revascularized). He develops acute onset severe dyspnea with O2 saturation 82%. A new loud holosystolic murmur is heard at the apex.
What exam would you perform? Focused cardiac ultrasound — mitral valve, LV function.






Tip



Video slot: Loops for interpretation.


What you see: Inferior and posterior wall motion abnormality (known from prior). Posterior mitral leaflet flail segment. Large eccentric MR jet directed anteriorly along the interatrial septum. LA not dilated. Hyperdynamic LV.
How does this change management? Acute severe MR from posterior papillary muscle rupture — a mechanical complication of inferior MI. This is a surgical emergency. The non-dilated LA with acute, massive MR means LA pressure is rising rapidly — the patient is heading toward cardiogenic shock. Call CT surgery immediately. Nitroprusside to reduce afterload as a bridge. IABP to augment forward flow. Do not delay for catheterization — go to the OR.



Case 3: Right heart failure with elevated RVSP
Clinical scenario: A 55-year-old woman with systemic sclerosis presents with progressive exertional dyspnea and lower extremity edema. JVD is present. She has a soft systolic murmur at the left lower sternal border.
What exam would you perform? Focused cardiac ultrasound with TR jet interrogation.






Tip



Video slot: Loops for interpretation.


What you see: Dilated RA and RV. TR jet on color Doppler. CW Doppler peak TR velocity 4.2 m/s. IVC 2.3 cm, non-collapsing (estimated RAP 15 mmHg). RVSP = 4(4.2)² + 15 = 71 + 15 = 86 mmHg.
How does this change management? Severe pulmonary hypertension (RVSP 86 mmHg). In a patient with systemic sclerosis, pulmonary arterial hypertension is a known complication and a major cause of mortality. Refer urgently to a pulmonary hypertension center. Right heart catheterization is required to confirm diagnosis and guide therapy. Begin PAH-targeted therapy (phosphodiesterase inhibitor or endothelin receptor antagonist) in consultation with a specialist.






Tip



Case format reminder: The case ends with a management decision, not just a diagnosis.

title: Module 7 — Basic Valve Assessment
text:
Quiz
Anki deck for spaced repetition: link coming soon.






Note



Q1. On PLAX, you see the anterior mitral leaflet taking on a curved “hockey stick” shape in diastole. What is the diagnosis and what is the hemodynamic consequence?






Caution





Answer Mitral stenosis. The hockey stick deformity results from rheumatic commissural fusion — the leaflet body is pliable but the tip is tethered. The hemodynamic consequence is obstruction to diastolic LV filling, causing elevated LA pressure, LA dilation, pulmonary hypertension, and reduced cardiac output. Atrial fibrillation and tachycardia are particularly poorly tolerated because they reduce diastolic filling time.



Q2. How do you estimate RVSP from tricuspid regurgitation, and what are the limitations?






Caution





Answer RVSP = 4 × (peak TR velocity in m/s)² + estimated RAP. RAP is estimated from IVC size and collapsibility. Limitations: requires a well-aligned CW Doppler beam parallel to the TR jet (off-axis measurements underestimate velocity); in severe TR with elevated RA pressure, the RV-RA gradient may be low (low TR velocity) despite severe RV failure; requires a measurable TR jet (not all patients have one).



Q3. A patient with acute aortic regurgitation has premature mitral valve closure on M-mode. What does this finding mean physiologically?






Caution





Answer Premature mitral valve closure means the diastolic LV pressure has risen above LA pressure before atrial contraction — the LV is so volume-loaded that it closes the mitral valve early. This indicates critically elevated LVEDP, impending hemodynamic collapse, and the urgent need for surgical intervention. It is one of the most ominous signs in acute AR.



Q4. Why is color Doppler alone unreliable for grading the severity of an eccentric MR jet?






Caution





Answer Eccentric jets (Coanda effect) hug the atrial wall, constrained by the wall’s boundary layer, and appear smaller than they are on color Doppler. A wall-hugging jet may be severe despite a small apparent color area. Other clues to severe MR — pulmonary edema out of proportion to LV function, hyperdynamic LV, non-dilated LA in acute presentation, or a clearly visible flail segment — should raise suspicion even when the jet appears small.



Q5. Why are vasodilators dangerous in severe aortic stenosis?






Caution





Answer In severe AS, the aortic valve is the fixed obstruction to outflow. Cardiac output cannot increase in proportion to the drop in systemic vascular resistance caused by vasodilators. The result is a precipitous drop in blood pressure without a compensatory increase in cardiac output. Vasodilators should be avoided or used with extreme caution in severe AS; the definitive treatment is relieving the obstruction.

title: Module 5 — IVC & Volume Status
text:
What clinical question does this exam answer, and how do findings change management?






Note



The bedside decision frame: Two questions in order.

Is this patient likely to respond to a fluid bolus? A collapsible, small IVC in a spontaneously breathing patient suggests low right-sided filling pressure and likely fluid responsiveness. A plethoric, non-collapsing IVC suggests elevated venous pressure — giving fluid will not help and may cause harm.
Is there venous congestion? An elevated IVC diameter with loss of respiratory variation, combined with hepatic vein dilation and portal vein pulsatility, indicates systemic venous hypertension. This pattern shifts the frame from “give fluid” to “treat the cause of congestion.”



The IVC is the most accessible venous structure for bedside hemodynamic assessment. It is also the most misused. A collapsible IVC does not guarantee that a fluid bolus will improve cardiac output — it indicates that the right atrial pressure is low, which is one of several conditions necessary for fluid responsiveness. Equally important, a plethoric IVC is not always tamponade — it can reflect right heart failure, PE, severe tricuspid regurgitation, or aggressive fluid resuscitation. The IVC is one data point in a hemodynamic assessment, not a standalone decision-maker.

title: Module 5 — IVC & Volume Status
text:
2. Image acquisition
Probe, windows, and technique for this module.
Use a phased array or curvilinear probe from the subcostal window. The IVC enters the right atrium from below. The image plane is optimized to show the IVC in its long axis as it traverses the liver toward the RA.


Subcostal IVC view






Tip



Video slot: IVC acquisition — probe position, long axis of the IVC, measurement technique, respiratory variation.



Probe placement: Subcostal, indicator to the patient’s right (or toward the head depending on your convention), angled to bring the IVC into view as it enters the RA. The hepatic vein confluence should be visible entering the IVC.
Measurement: IVC diameter is measured 2 cm from the RA-IVC junction. Measure at end-expiration for the resting diameter, then assess collapse with a sniff (spontaneous breathing) or the distensibility index (mechanical ventilation).
Common error: Imaging the aorta instead of the IVC. The IVC is to the patient’s right of midline, collapses with inspiration, and enters the RA. The aorta is to the left, pulsatile, and does not collapse.



Hepatic vein assessment






Tip



Video slot: Hepatic vein PW Doppler — normal anterograde flow vs diastolic flow reversal in venous congestion.


Probe placement: Same subcostal window, angle to bring the hepatic veins into view entering the IVC. Sample volume placed in the hepatic vein 1–2 cm from the IVC junction.
What you are looking for: Normal hepatic vein flow is predominantly anterograde (systolic and diastolic waves toward the RA) with small physiologic reversals. Diastolic flow reversal prominent with expiration suggests elevated right-sided filling pressure (constrictive physiology). Systolic flow reversal suggests severe tricuspid regurgitation.



Portal vein pulsatility






Tip



Video slot: Portal vein PW Doppler — normally monophasic flow vs pulsatile flow in severe venous congestion.


What you are looking for: The portal vein normally has continuous, mildly pulsatile anterograde flow. When systemic venous pressure is severely elevated, this flow becomes markedly pulsatile or even reverses — a sign of severe venous congestion transmitted to the portal system. Portal vein pulsatility fraction >50% is associated with worse outcomes in ICU patients and in those with right heart failure.

title: Module 5 — IVC & Volume Status
text:
3. Normal & normal variants






Tip



Video slots: Normal IVC — diameter 1.5–2.1 cm, >50% collapsibility with sniff. IVC in an athlete (mildly enlarged but still collapsible).



Normal IVC
Diameter 1.5–2.1 cm at end-expiration, with greater than 50% collapsibility with a maximal sniff or inspiration. This corresponds to an estimated RA pressure of 0–5 mmHg.


The athlete’s IVC
Well-trained athletes may have mildly enlarged IVCs (up to 2.5 cm) at rest due to increased plasma volume and vagal tone, with preserved or even exaggerated collapsibility. Clinical context is essential — a large IVC in a healthy, euvolemic runner is not the same as a large IVC in a patient with right heart failure.


IVC in mechanically ventilated patients
Respiratory variation is reversed in mechanically ventilated patients — the IVC distends with positive pressure insufflation (during inspiration) and collapses with expiration. Use the distensibility index rather than collapsibility: (IVC max − IVC min) / IVC min × 100%. A distensibility index greater than 18% predicts fluid responsiveness in passively ventilated patients without spontaneous breathing efforts. This rule does not apply if the patient is triggering the ventilator, has high PEEP, or has low tidal volumes (<8 mL/kg).

title: Module 5 — IVC & Volume Status
text:
4. Pathology library
Organized by finding, not by diagnosis.

Small, collapsible IVC






Tip



Video slot: Small IVC — diameter <1.5 cm, >50% collapse, “flat” appearance.



Diameter less than 1.5 cm with greater than 50% respiratory collapse. Estimated RA pressure 0–5 mmHg.
Teaching points:

Consistent with hypovolemia, distributive shock, or effective diuresis.
In a hypotensive patient, a small collapsible IVC suggests volume responsiveness and supports a cautious fluid trial.
Does not guarantee that fluid will improve cardiac output — also requires adequate LV and RV function to translate preload into stroke volume.
Serial assessment after a fluid bolus (did the IVC change? did cardiac output improve?) is more informative than a single measurement.




Plethoric, non-collapsing IVC






Tip



Video slot: Plethoric IVC — diameter >2.1 cm, <50% collapse, associated with elevated RA pressure.



Diameter greater than 2.1 cm with less than 50% respiratory collapse. Estimated RA pressure 10–20 mmHg.
Teaching points:

Does not equal tamponade — this is one finding among several. Always assess for chamber collapse and clinical context.
Causes: right heart failure, massive PE, cardiac tamponade, constrictive pericarditis, severe TR, aggressive fluid resuscitation, high PEEP.
In this setting, additional fluid boluses are unlikely to be beneficial and may worsen venous congestion.
The priority is identifying and treating the cause of elevated RA pressure.




Venous congestion pattern






Tip



Video slots: - Plethoric IVC with diastolic hepatic vein flow reversal - Pulsatile portal vein flow


A syndrome of IVC dilation, hepatic vein abnormalities, and portal vein pulsatility reflecting severe systemic venous hypertension. Associated with worse outcomes in patients with right heart failure, cardiogenic shock, and septic shock.
Teaching points:

Venous congestion causes end-organ dysfunction — congested kidneys, a congested liver, and a congested gut are not simply “full,” they are physiologically impaired.
Recognition of venous congestion should prompt de-escalation of fluid administration and active decongestion (diuresis, ultrafiltration) even in patients who appear to need more fluid for other reasons.
The RVSP-VExUS framework (combining IVC, hepatic vein, and portal vein findings) grades congestion severity and has prognostic implications.




Intermediate IVC
Diameter 1.5–2.1 cm with variable collapse. Estimated RA pressure 5–10 mmHg. This is the most common and least definitive finding — the IVC alone cannot reliably predict fluid responsiveness in this range.
Teaching points:

Use dynamic assessments instead: passive leg raise (PLR) with cardiac output monitoring, or a mini-fluid challenge with serial stroke volume measurement.
A PLR that transiently increases stroke volume (or pulse pressure) by >10% predicts fluid responsiveness with high sensitivity and specificity, regardless of IVC status.
Do not make a high-stakes fluid decision based on an intermediate IVC in isolation.

title: Module 5 — IVC & Volume Status
text:
5. Integration cases
Cases where the finding changes management.


Case 1: Septic shock — is this patient fluid responsive?
Clinical scenario: A 72-year-old woman with urosepsis has received 3 L of crystalloid and is on norepinephrine 0.2 mcg/kg/min. BP is 84/52, HR 112. Lactate is 4.1 mmol/L and trending up slightly. The team is debating another fluid bolus.
What exam would you perform? Focused cardiac ultrasound with IVC assessment.






Tip



Video slot: Loops for interpretation.


What you see: IVC 1.4 cm with >70% collapse on sniff. LV hyperdynamic. RV normal size. No effusion.
How does this change management? Small, collapsible IVC with hyperdynamic LV — consistent with distributive physiology and likely fluid responsiveness. Administer a cautious fluid bolus (250–500 mL) and reassess. If lactate clears and hemodynamics improve, the fluid was beneficial. If not, escalate vasopressor therapy rather than continuing to fluid load. The hyperdynamic LV argues against a cardiogenic component.



Case 2: The patient who won’t respond to fluids
Clinical scenario: An 80-year-old man with CHF (EF 25%) and pneumonia is admitted with hypotension. He has received 2 L of saline. BP remains 86/54. Creatinine is rising. He has bilateral crackles.
What exam would you perform? Focused cardiac ultrasound with IVC and hepatic vein assessment.






Tip



Video slot: Loops for interpretation.


What you see: IVC 2.6 cm, non-collapsing. Plethoric hepatic veins with diastolic flow reversal. Pulsatile portal vein. Severely reduced EF. Bilateral pleural effusions.
How does this change management? Stop fluids immediately — this patient is severely congested and has cardiogenic shock. The rising creatinine is from renal venous congestion, not from hypovolemia. Additional fluid will worsen pulmonary edema and organ congestion further. Initiate dobutamine for inotropic support. Cautious diuresis to reduce venous congestion. Consider early nephrology involvement if oliguria persists despite decongestion.



Case 3: Post-resuscitation — how much fluid did this patient get?
Clinical scenario: A 55-year-old man is post-arrest, now intubated and sedated. He received 4 L during the resuscitation. BP on norepinephrine is 92/60. The ICU team is reviewing hemodynamic targets.
What exam would you perform? Focused cardiac ultrasound with IVC distensibility assessment (mechanically ventilated).






Tip



Video slot: Loops for interpretation.


What you see: IVC 2.3 cm. Distensibility index 10% (below the 18% threshold). Normal LV function. RV mildly enlarged.
How does this change management? Not fluid responsive by distensibility criteria. The patient received significant resuscitation volume and the RV is mildly enlarged. Avoid additional fluid boluses. Hold further resuscitation fluid. Focus on optimizing vasopressor titration and monitoring end-organ recovery. Reassess in 4–6 hours.



Case 4: Distinguishing cardiogenic from septic shock with the IVC
Clinical scenario: A 68-year-old man with no known cardiac history is brought in with BP 76/44, HR 118, and altered mental status. Temp 38.9°C. Lactate 5.2 mmol/L. The team is debating whether to give fluid or start inotropes.
What exam would you perform? Focused cardiac ultrasound — LV, RV, IVC.






Tip



Video slot: Loops for interpretation.


What you see: Severely reduced EF. Globally hypokinetic LV, not dilated. IVC 2.4 cm, non-collapsing. No effusion. Mild RV dilation.
How does this change management? This is not septic shock with a responsive ventricle — it is cardiogenic shock (or mixed shock with a dominant cardiogenic component), likely sepsis-induced cardiomyopathy or a new ischemic event. The plethoric IVC confirms elevated filling pressures. Start dobutamine. Limit fluids to what is required for medication delivery. Obtain an ECG and troponin. Investigate the cause of the cardiomyopathy — myocarditis, ischemia, and sepsis-induced depression are all in the differential.






Tip



Case format reminder: The case ends with a management decision, not just a diagnosis.

title: Module 5 — IVC & Volume Status
text:
Quiz
Anki deck for spaced repetition: link coming soon.






Note



Q1. A patient has an IVC of 1.8 cm with 40% collapse. What does this tell you about fluid responsiveness?






Caution





Answer An intermediate IVC (1.5–2.1 cm) with intermediate collapse is not reliably predictive of fluid responsiveness in either direction. Do not make a high-stakes fluid decision based on this alone. Use a dynamic test instead — passive leg raise with cardiac output monitoring, or a mini-fluid challenge (100–250 mL) with serial stroke volume or pulse pressure assessment.



Q2. How does the IVC behave differently in a mechanically ventilated patient compared to a spontaneously breathing patient?






Caution





Answer In spontaneous breathing, the IVC collapses with inspiration (negative intrathoracic pressure increases venous return). In mechanical ventilation, the IVC distends with insufflation (positive pressure reduces venous return). Use the distensibility index in ventilated patients: (IVC max − IVC min) / IVC min >18% predicts responsiveness. This only applies to passive ventilation without spontaneous efforts and at tidal volumes ≥8 mL/kg.



Q3. What is the clinical significance of a pulsatile portal vein on Doppler?






Caution





Answer Marked portal vein pulsatility (pulsatility fraction >50%) indicates severe systemic venous hypertension transmitted to the portal circulation. It is associated with end-organ congestion (renal, hepatic), worse clinical outcomes, and suggests that further fluid administration is likely harmful. It is a key component of the VExUS congestion assessment framework.



Q4. A patient in septic shock has a plethoric IVC. A colleague suggests giving another fluid bolus because “the lactate is still elevated.” How do you respond?






Caution





Answer A plethoric, non-collapsing IVC indicates elevated right atrial pressure — the patient is not preload-deficient. Giving more fluid is unlikely to improve cardiac output and may worsen venous congestion, impairing organ perfusion. Elevated lactate in this context may reflect impaired hepatic lactate clearance from congestion, not ongoing tissue hypoperfusion from inadequate preload. Focus on treating the cause of the elevated filling pressure and optimize vasopressor or inotropic support.



Q5. You image the IVC and find a large, pulsatile structure to the left of the spine. What did you image, and how do you correct it?






Caution





Answer You imaged the descending aorta, not the IVC. The aorta is to the left of midline, is pulsatile (arterial waveform on Doppler), and does not communicate with the right atrium. To correct: move slightly to the right of midline, angle toward the right atrium, and look for the structure that enters the RA from below with a venous waveform on Doppler.

title: Module 3 — Right Ventricular Function
text:
What clinical question does this exam answer, and how do findings change management?






Note



The bedside decision frame: Two questions in order.

Is the RV dilated or failing? A visually enlarged RV — approaching or exceeding the size of the LV — is the primary finding. Normal RV is roughly two-thirds the size of the LV on apical four-chamber view.
What is the cause, and does it require immediate intervention? RV failure from massive PE is a needle/catheter emergency. RV failure from chronic pulmonary hypertension or ARDS needs a different approach. The echo does not always give you the diagnosis — it gives you the hemodynamic phenotype to guide management.



The RV is the chamber most often underappreciated in critical care. It operates as a low-pressure, high-compliance structure that tolerates volume overload relatively well but is exquisitely sensitive to acute pressure increases. When RV afterload rises acutely — as in massive PE — the RV dilates rapidly, shifts the interventricular septum, impairs LV filling, and drives the patient into obstructive shock. Recognizing this pattern quickly and accurately is one of the highest-yield skills in critical care echo.
