title: Module 6 — Integration
text:
4. When findings conflict
The exam doesn’t always give you a clean answer.






Tip



Video slot: Mixed shock state — reduced EF with small IVC; how to interpret and what to do.


Common conflicting scenarios and how to reason through them:
Reduced EF + small IVC The LV is failing but filling pressures are low — the patient is hypovolemic relative to their baseline. A cautious fluid trial (250 mL) may improve preload and cardiac output without tipping into pulmonary edema. Monitor closely.
Hyperdynamic LV + plethoric IVC High-output state with elevated venous pressure. Consider: severe sepsis with right heart congestion, severe tricuspid regurgitation, hepatic disease, or a patient in compensated high-output heart failure who has been aggressively fluid-loaded.
Normal LV + dilated RV + plethoric IVC (no effusion) Obstructive physiology from PE or acute cor pulmonale from ARDS. Do not give more fluid. Focus on diagnosis and afterload reduction.
Large effusion + no tamponade physiology + plethoric IVC Consider chronic effusion (malignant, uremic) with concomitant right heart failure causing the elevated IVC — these are two separate problems. Treat both.

title: Module 6 — Integration
text:
5. Serial exams and trending
Echo is not a one-time test.






Tip



Video slot: Before/after comparison — echo before and after 1 L fluid bolus in a patient with septic shock.


The true power of bedside echo in critical care is the ability to perform serial exams and track the response to interventions in real time. Key scenarios for repeat assessment:

After a fluid bolus: Did IVC diameter change? Did cardiac output improve (visual or measured)? Did venous congestion worsen?
After vasopressor dose change: Did LV or RV filling improve?
After diuresis: Is venous congestion resolving? Is IVC size decreasing?
After pericardiocentesis: Is tamponade physiology resolved? Is there residual constrictive physiology?
Trending over hours: Is RV function improving with treatment of PE or ARDS? Is EF recovering in myocarditis?

Each exam should be compared to the prior exam, not interpreted in isolation. Document the key findings (EF category, RV:LV ratio, IVC diameter, IVC collapsibility) so that trends are visible across shifts.

title: Module 6 — Integration
text:
6. Integration cases
Complex cases requiring synthesis of all modules.


Case 1: The patient in undifferentiated shock
Clinical scenario: A 64-year-old man with no significant cardiac history is transferred from a community hospital with “septic shock, possible PE.” He has been on norepinephrine for 6 hours and received 5 L of crystalloid. On arrival: BP 74/48, HR 128, temp 37.8°C, O2 sat 90% on 6 L NC. He is slightly confused. Chest X-ray shows bilateral infiltrates. Troponin is mildly elevated.
Systematic four-question exam:






Tip



Video slot: Loops for interpretation — complete four-window exam.


What you see: 1. No pericardial effusion. 2. LV severely reduced EF. Global hypokinesis, no RWMA. 3. RV moderately dilated. D-sign present. McConnell’s sign absent. TAPSE 14 mm. 4. IVC 2.5 cm, non-collapsing.
Integration: This is not simple septic shock. The severely reduced LV EF with RV dilation and a plethoric IVC suggests biventricular failure. The bilateral infiltrates could reflect pulmonary edema rather than pneumonia. The elevated troponin is consistent with cardiogenic shock. The differential includes new dilated cardiomyopathy with acute decompensation, fulminant myocarditis, or sepsis-induced biventricular dysfunction.
How does this change management? Stop fluids — the patient is congested. Add dobutamine for inotropic support. Get a 12-lead ECG and urgent formal echo. Consider PA catheter to characterize hemodynamics. The “sepsis” label may be wrong — treat aggressively for a primary cardiac event. If troponin is significantly elevated and ECG shows ischemic changes, activate the cath lab.



Case 2: Post-arrest resuscitation — what caused the arrest?
Clinical scenario: A 58-year-old woman had a witnessed cardiac arrest in the hospital corridor. She was resuscitated in 8 minutes with 2 shocks and CPR. Now intubated, hemodynamically marginal on vasopressors. No prior cardiac history. The team wants to know: VF arrest from ACS, PE, or something else?
Systematic four-question exam:






Tip



Video slot: Loops for interpretation.



What you see: 1. No effusion. 2. LV: anterior and apical wall akinesis. Severely reduced EF. No global hypokinesis — the inferior and lateral walls move. 3. RV: normal size. No D-sign. Normal TAPSE. 4. IVC: 2.0 cm, 30% collapse (borderline).
Integration: Regional wall motion abnormality in the anterior/LAD distribution with a normal RV. This is a large anterior STEMI causing VF arrest. The RV is not dilated — this is not a PE causing the arrest. The IVC is borderline, consistent with post-resuscitation state.
How does this change management? Activate the cath lab immediately for emergent PCI. This is STEMI-equivalent post-arrest — coronary angiography is indicated regardless of the post-resuscitation ECG. Initiate targeted temperature management per protocol. The echo finding of an anterior RWMA pointing to the LAD is the critical finding that directs the team to the right intervention.



Case 3: Hypoxic respiratory failure — cardiac or pulmonary?
Clinical scenario: A 71-year-old woman with COPD is admitted with progressive dyspnea over 3 days. She is hypoxic (O2 sat 84% on 10 L), hypotensive (BP 90/60), and has bilateral crackles and lower extremity edema. BNP is 1,800 pg/mL. Chest X-ray shows bilateral opacities. The team is debating whether to intubate for COPD exacerbation or initiate diuresis for decompensated heart failure.
Systematic four-question exam:






Tip



Video slot: Loops for interpretation.


What you see: 1. No effusion. 2. LV: severely reduced EF, dilated — chronic appearance. 3. RV: moderately dilated. D-sign (diastolic flattening, consistent with volume overload). 4. IVC: 2.8 cm, non-collapsing. Hepatic veins dilated.
Integration: Decompensated heart failure with reduced EF, biventricular volume overload, and severe congestion — not a primary COPD exacerbation. The COPD may be contributing to increased RV afterload, but the dominant pathophysiology is cardiogenic pulmonary edema.
How does this change management? Initiate NIV (BiPAP) to reduce preload and work of breathing. Begin aggressive diuresis. Add dobutamine if hemodynamics do not improve with afterload and preload reduction. Do not intubate for COPD management — the indication, if intubation becomes necessary, is respiratory failure from cardiogenic pulmonary edema. Treat the heart.



Case 4: The patient who “isn’t responding” to treatment
Clinical scenario: A 77-year-old man with known COPD and newly diagnosed lung cancer was admitted 3 days ago for presumed COPD exacerbation. He has been on bronchodilators, steroids, and antibiotics with minimal improvement. He remains hypoxic and increasingly vasopressor-dependent. Repeat echo is requested by the ICU attending.
Systematic four-question exam:






Tip



Video slot: Loops for interpretation.


What you see: 1. Moderate pericardial effusion. No RA or RV collapse. IVC plethoric. 2. LV: normal EF. No RWMA. 3. RV: moderately dilated. D-sign present (pressure overload pattern — systolic flattening). 4. IVC: 2.4 cm, non-collapsing.
Integration: Two separate findings: a pericardial effusion (likely malignant) and RV pressure overload without tamponade physiology. The effusion is not causing tamponade. The RV dilation with pressure-overload D-sign in a patient with lung cancer raises the possibility of pulmonary hypertension from tumor invasion, PE, or extrinsic pulmonary vascular compression. Neither finding fits a primary COPD exacerbation.
How does this change management? CT pulmonary angiography to evaluate for PE and pulmonary vascular involvement by tumor. Oncology consultation for the effusion (malignant pericardial effusion likely). Reframe the clinical diagnosis — this is not a COPD exacerbation. The failure to respond to bronchodilators and steroids was a clue that the diagnosis was wrong.



Case 5: The post-operative patient who won’t come off the ventilator
Clinical scenario: A 69-year-old man undergoes elective aortic valve replacement. He is extubated on post-op day 2 but reintubated 6 hours later for respiratory failure. He is now post-op day 5, sedated, and failing repeated extubation trials. An ICU team requests bedside echo to evaluate hemodynamics.
Systematic four-question exam:






Tip



Video slot: Loops for interpretation — post-surgical windows (often challenging).


What you see: 1. Small anterior effusion. No chamber collapse. 2. LV: EF 45% (mildly reduced, new compared to pre-op 60%). Anterior wall motion mildly reduced. 3. RV: mildly dilated. TAPSE 14 mm. 4. IVC: 2.2 cm, 20% distensibility (borderline for fluid responsiveness in a ventilated patient).
Integration: New mild LV dysfunction (post-operative stunned myocardium vs perioperative MI), mild RV dysfunction, and borderline volume status. The anterior wall motion abnormality raises concern for a perioperative LAD event. The ventricular dysfunction is driving respiratory failure — the patient is not failing extubation from pulmonary mechanics but from hemodynamic compromise.
How does this change management? Obtain an ECG and serial troponins — a perioperative MI must be ruled out. Cardiology consultation for post-surgical echo. Optimize hemodynamics: gentle diuresis to reduce preload, optimize heart rate, consider low-dose inotrope if EF remains depressed. Address the cardiac problem before the next extubation trial — the respiratory failure is a symptom, not the diagnosis.






Tip



Integration reminder: The power of the four-question exam is not in any single finding. It is in the composite picture and the management decision that follows.

title: Module 6 — Integration
text:
Quiz
Anki deck for spaced repetition: link coming soon.






Note



Q1. A patient in shock has a hyperdynamic LV, a dilated RV with D-sign, and a plethoric IVC. No pericardial effusion. What is the most likely hemodynamic phenotype and the priority intervention?






Caution





Answer Obstructive shock from pulmonary embolism (or acute cor pulmonale). The hyperdynamic LV is underfilled due to RV failure impairing output. The priority is reducing RV afterload — systemic anticoagulation, and in hemodynamic collapse, systemic thrombolytics or catheter-directed therapy. Do not give fluid boluses.



Q2. You find a severely reduced EF and a small, collapsible IVC in a hypotensive patient. What does this suggest and how do you manage it?






Caution





Answer The LV is failing but filling pressures are low — cardiogenic shock superimposed on hypovolemia (or volume depletion from prior diuresis/bleeding). A cautious fluid challenge (250 mL) may improve preload and cardiac output. Monitor closely for pulmonary edema. Add inotropic support if the EF does not improve with preload optimization.



Q3. After performing a bedside echo, you are unsure whether the reduced EF is new or chronic. How does the LV size help you distinguish?






Caution





Answer A dilated LV suggests a chronic process — the heart has had time to remodel. A non-dilated LV with severely reduced EF suggests an acute process (myocarditis, Takotsubo, acute MI, sepsis-induced cardiomyopathy). Acuity changes the differential and the urgency of investigation (e.g., emergent cath lab for suspected acute MI vs. supportive management for myocarditis).



Q4. A patient’s echo shows: no effusion, normal LV, dilated RV with McConnell’s sign, plethoric IVC. What is the diagnosis and what is the single most important intervention?






Caution





Answer Massive pulmonary embolism with RV failure. The single most important intervention is systemic thrombolysis (if no contraindication) — it rapidly reduces RV afterload by dissolving the clot. Anticoagulation alone is insufficient in hemodynamic collapse. Activate a PE response team or get interventional radiology and cardiac surgery on the line simultaneously.



Q5. What is the purpose of serial bedside echo in the ICU, and what should be documented to make serial exams useful?






Caution





Answer Serial echo tracks the response to interventions and identifies deterioration or recovery over time. A single exam is a snapshot; serial exams reveal trajectory. Document key quantitative or semi-quantitative findings at each exam: EF category (severely reduced / mildly reduced / normal / hyperdynamic), RV:LV ratio, IVC diameter and collapsibility, presence of chamber collapse or D-sign. This allows any clinician picking up the patient to immediately understand where the hemodynamics started and where they are now.

title: Module 8 — Lung Ultrasound
text:
What clinical question does this exam answer, and how do findings change management?






Note



The bedside decision frame: In a patient with dyspnea or hypoxia, four questions in order.

Is there a pneumothorax? Absent lung sliding with a barcode sign and a lung point = pneumothorax until proven otherwise. This is the first question because it is immediately life-threatening and immediately treatable.
Is there a pleural effusion? An anechoic, layering collection with a sinusoid sign points to pleural fluid and may explain hypoxia or guide drainage.
Are there bilateral B-lines? Diffuse bilateral B-lines indicate interstitial edema — either cardiogenic (flash pulmonary edema) or inflammatory (ARDS, pneumonitis).
Is there consolidation? Hepatization of lung tissue with air or fluid bronchograms points to pneumonia, atelectasis, or lobar collapse.



Lung ultrasound is more accurate than chest X-ray for detecting pneumothorax, pleural effusion, and consolidation at the bedside. It is real-time, radiation-free, and available immediately. The BLUE protocol (Bedside Lung Ultrasound in Emergency) provides a structured framework that yields a diagnosis in the majority of patients with acute respiratory failure within minutes.

text:
2. Image acquisition
Probe, windows, and technique for this module.
Probe selection depends on the target: - Pneumothorax: High-frequency linear probe (7–15 MHz) — superior resolution of the pleural line. - B-lines, effusion, consolidation: Phased array or curvilinear probe (3–5 MHz) — greater depth penetration. - In practice, a single curvilinear or phased array probe is adequate for a complete lung exam if a linear probe is not available.
Patient positioning: Supine for trauma/ICU. Lateral decubitus or sitting forward improves posterior basal views. The posterior lateral alveolar and/or pleural (PLAPS) point is the single highest-yield location for effusion and consolidation in a supine patient.


Probe placement — the BLUE zones






Tip



Video slot: BLUE zone anatomy — upper BLUE point, lower BLUE point, PLAPS point on a supine patient.


Upper BLUE point: Upper third of the anterior chest, between the clavicle and the nipple line, midclavicular.
Lower BLUE point: Lower third of the anterior chest, same column.
PLAPS point: Posterior lateral alveolar and/or pleural syndrome point — lateral chest wall, at the level of the lower BLUE point, continued posteriorly. This is the dependent zone in a supine patient and the most sensitive location for both effusion and consolidation.



Scanning technique
Place the probe perpendicular to the ribs with the indicator toward the patient’s head. Two adjacent rib shadows (“bat sign”) frame the pleural line, which appears as a bright horizontal echogenic line approximately 0.5 cm below the skin surface. All artifacts (A-lines, B-lines) originate from the pleural line.

title: Module 8 — Lung Ultrasound
text:
3. Normal & normal variants






Tip



Video slots: Normal lung sliding — the “seashore sign” on M-mode; A-lines; the bat sign.





Lung sliding
The visceral and parietal pleura glide against each other with each breath — this appears as a shimmering, dynamic motion at the pleural line. On M-mode, the resulting pattern is the seashore sign: a granular “sandy beach” pattern below the pleural line (moving lung) and horizontal lines above (static chest wall).
Lung sliding = visceral and parietal pleura are in contact. Its presence rules out pneumothorax at that probe position.


A-lines
Horizontal, equidistant reverberation artifacts below the pleural line, occurring at multiples of the skin-to-pleural distance. A-lines are a normal finding — they arise from reverberation of the ultrasound beam off the air-filled lung surface. A-lines + lung sliding = normal aerated lung.


Lung pulse
In the apneic or intubated patient, cardiac pulsations transmitted through the lung may substitute for respiratory lung sliding as a way to confirm pleural apposition. The lung pulse = no pneumothorax at that point.

title: Module 8 — Lung Ultrasound
text:
4. Pathology library
Organized by finding.

B-lines (interstitial syndrome)






Tip



Video slots: - Single B-line vs multiple confluent B-lines - Bilateral anterior B-lines — cardiogenic pulmonary edema pattern - Focal unilateral B-lines — pneumonia or contusion pattern



B-lines are vertical, laser-like artifacts that: - Arise from the pleural line - Extend to the bottom of the screen without fading - Move with lung sliding - Erase A-lines
Grading: - 0–2 B-lines per zone: normal - 3 or more B-lines per zone: interstitial syndrome (thickened interlobular septa, subpleural edema) - Confluent (“white lung”): severe alveolar edema
Distribution is the key differentiator:



Pattern
Likely Diagnosis




Bilateral anterior, homogeneous
Cardiogenic pulmonary edema


Bilateral anterior, heterogeneous
ARDS


Focal, unilateral
Pneumonia, contusion, atelectasis


Posterior only
Early interstitial edema, passive atelectasis



Teaching points:

B-lines are dynamic — they decrease with diuresis in cardiogenic edema and can be tracked serially to assess treatment response.
Homogeneous bilateral anterior B-lines in a patient with reduced LV EF = flash pulmonary edema. Give diuretics and afterload reduction, not antibiotics.
Heterogeneous or unilateral B-lines should not be attributed to cardiogenic edema without additional context.




Pleural effusion






Tip



Video slots: - Anechoic effusion at the PLAPS point — “quad sign” - Sinusoid sign on M-mode - Echogenic effusion (exudate, hemothorax) - Atelectatic lung floating within an effusion



Pleural effusion appears as an anechoic (or hypoechoic) space between the visceral and parietal pleura, typically in the dependent (posterior) zones in a supine patient.
Key findings:

Quad sign: Four sides of an anechoic quadrilateral — rib shadows on either side, parietal pleura above, visceral pleura below. Pathognomonic of effusion.
Sinusoid sign: On M-mode at the PLAPS point, the lung moves toward the pleural line with inspiration (like a sinusoid wave) — confirms fluid between the pleural layers.
Floating atelectatic lung: The collapsed lung may be seen floating within the effusion — confirms it is fluid and identifies atelectatic lung vs consolidation.

Effusion characterization: - Anechoic: transudates, early exudates - Echogenic or septated: exudates, empyema, hemothorax - “Swirling” particles: empyema, chylothorax
Volume estimation: Effusion depth (cm) × 20 = approximate volume (mL) for a moderate free-flowing effusion — rough approximation only.
Teaching points:

Posterior effusions are missed on supine chest X-ray until they exceed ~500 mL. Ultrasound detects effusions as small as 20 mL.
Loculated effusions do not layer dependently — the fluid does not shift when the patient is repositioned.
Echogenic or complex fluid requires drainage with a chest tube, not a simple needle.
Always mark the site for thoracentesis under ultrasound guidance (see Module 11).




Pneumothorax






Tip



Video slots: - Absent lung sliding — the “stratosphere” or “barcode” sign on M-mode - Lung point — the transition from absent to present sliding - Normal sliding for comparison


Pneumothorax separates the pleural layers with air, eliminating lung sliding.
Key findings:

Absent lung sliding: The pleural line is still visible, but there is no dynamic motion beneath it. A-lines may be present. The seashore sign is replaced by the barcode (stratosphere) sign on M-mode — horizontal lines throughout (no sandy beach).
Lung point: The transition zone between pneumothorax (no sliding) and normal lung (sliding present). The lung point is specific (nearly 100%) for pneumothorax — if you find it, the diagnosis is confirmed. Its lateral position correlates with pneumothorax size.
Absent B-lines: B-lines require pleural apposition to form. Their presence at a given location rules out pneumothorax at that location.

Conditions that abolish lung sliding without pneumothorax: - Mainstem intubation (sliding absent on the unventilated side) - Apnea (no respiratory motion — lung pulse may substitute) - Severe ARDS (severely reduced lung compliance) - Pleural adhesions, prior pleurodesis
Teaching points:

Lung sliding present = no pneumothorax at that probe position. A normal anterior exam does not rule out a small posterior pneumothorax.
In tension pneumothorax with hemodynamic collapse, ultrasound is too slow — decompress first, image later.
In a ventilated patient, absent sliding on one side after intubation = mainstem intubation until proven otherwise. Pull the ETT back, reassess.




Consolidation






Tip



Video slots: - Hepatization — tissue-like echogenicity replacing aerated lung - Dynamic air bronchograms — moving bright foci within consolidation - Static air bronchograms — fixed bright foci - Fluid bronchograms — anechoic branching structures within consolidation



When lung loses air, it becomes echogenic and tissue-like (“hepatization” — looks like liver). Consolidation is visible when it extends to the pleural surface.
Key findings:

Hepatization: Echogenic, tissue-density structure where aerated lung should be. Loss of A-lines.
Air bronchograms: Bright echogenic foci within consolidation representing air in the bronchi.

Dynamic (moving with respiration): Indicates active ventilation — pneumonia with patent airways. Rules out complete obstruction.
Static (fixed): Suggests obstructive atelectasis or complete airspace consolidation (lobar pneumonia, ARDS).

Fluid bronchograms: Anechoic branching structures within consolidation — fluid-filled airways. Seen in severe pneumonia, lobar consolidation.

Distribution:

Posterior basal: passive atelectasis (common in ICU patients, position-dependent)
Any lobe: pneumonia
Entire lobe: lobar pneumonia or obstructive collapse (check for a mucus plug)

Teaching points:

Dynamic air bronchograms distinguish pneumonia (patent airways, active ventilation) from obstructive atelectasis (no bronchogram movement). This changes management — atelectasis needs suctioning or bronchoscopy, not antibiotics.
Consolidation + effusion = parapneumonic effusion until proven otherwise. Drain if complex.
Atelectasis from a displaced ETT resolves immediately upon ETT repositioning.

A structured diagnostic algorithm for acute respiratory failure.






Tip

The BLUE protocol (Lichtenstein & Mezière, 2008) uses lung ultrasound findings to identify the cause of acute respiratory failure with >90% accuracy.

title: Module 8 — Lung Ultrasound
text:
6. Integration cases
Cases where the finding changes management.


Case 1: Flash pulmonary edema vs pneumonia
Clinical scenario: A 72-year-old man with HTN and a history of HFrEF presents at 3 AM with acute dyspnea, O2 sat 82% on room air. He is diaphoretic and hypertensive (BP 198/110). CXR shows bilateral opacities. The admitting team is debating antibiotics vs diuretics.
What exam would you perform? Lung ultrasound — anterior and lateral zones bilaterally, plus cardiac echo.






Tip



Video slot: Loops for interpretation.


What you see: Bilateral anterior B-lines, homogeneous distribution, no sparing. No consolidation. Cardiac echo: severely reduced EF (known), small bilateral pleural effusions.
How does this change management? Bilateral homogeneous anterior B-lines + reduced EF + hypertension = hypertensive flash pulmonary edema. Give IV furosemide and IV nitroglycerin (afterload and preload reduction). Apply CPAP/BiPAP. Do not start antibiotics — there is no consolidation. Reassess B-lines after 1–2 hours of diuresis; clearing confirms cardiogenic etiology.



Case 2: Post-intubation hypoxia
Clinical scenario: A 45-year-old man is intubated for respiratory failure. After intubation, O2 saturation drops from 94% to 78%. Breath sounds are absent on the left. The RT is about to get a CXR.
What exam would you perform? Immediate lung ultrasound — bilateral anterior chest.






Tip



Video slot: Loops for interpretation.


What you see: Right: lung sliding present, A-lines. Left: absent lung sliding, barcode sign, no B-lines.
How does this change management? Mainstem intubation vs left pneumothorax. The clinical context (just intubated, sudden desaturation) makes mainstem intubation far more likely. Pull the ETT back 2 cm and reassess — if left sliding returns, this was a right mainstem intubation. If sliding remains absent and the patient is deteriorating, look for a lung point to confirm pneumothorax. Do not wait for CXR in a crashing patient.



Case 3: Trauma — FAST extension to lung
Clinical scenario: A 30-year-old man is brought in after a motorcycle collision. He is hemodynamically stable but has right chest wall contusions. CXR is being obtained. FAST exam shows no abdominal free fluid and no pericardial effusion.
What exam would you perform? Extended FAST (eFAST) — bilateral anterior lung assessment.






Tip



Video slot: Loops for interpretation.


What you see: Left: lung sliding, A-lines. Right: absent lung sliding anteriorly. Lung point identified at the mid-axillary line.
How does this change management? Right pneumothorax confirmed by lung point. The hemodynamically stable patient with a moderate pneumothorax (lung point at mid-axillary line) can be managed with a chest tube rather than needle decompression. Place a chest tube in the right chest. If the patient deteriorates hemodynamically, needle decompression first while preparing for the chest tube.



Case 4: ICU patient with new fever and hypoxia
Clinical scenario: An intubated 68-year-old man, post-op day 3 following major abdominal surgery, develops fever (38.8°C) and worsening hypoxia requiring FiO2 increase from 0.40 to 0.70.
What exam would you perform? Lung ultrasound — all zones bilaterally, PLAPS point.






Tip



Video slot: Loops for interpretation.


What you see: Left anterior zones: A-lines, lung sliding. Right anterior zones: A-lines, lung sliding. Right PLAPS: large area of consolidation with static air bronchograms. Small adjacent effusion.
How does this change management? Right lower lobe consolidation with static air bronchograms — likely right lower lobe pneumonia or obstructive atelectasis. The static bronchograms (not moving with respiration) raise concern for mucus plugging. Order bedside bronchoscopy to evaluate for mucus plug and obtain BAL for culture. If dynamic bronchograms were present (moving with respiration), this would be more consistent with pneumonia — start antibiotics. The distinction between static and dynamic bronchograms directs the next intervention.






Tip



Case format reminder: The case ends with a management decision, not just a diagnosis.

text:
Quiz
Anki deck for spaced repetition: link coming soon.






Note



Q1. What is a B-line, and how many are required per zone to indicate pathology?






Caution





Answer A B-line is a vertical, laser-like reverberation artifact arising from the pleural line, extending to the bottom of the screen without fading, moving with lung sliding, and erasing A-lines. Three or more B-lines per intercostal space is abnormal and indicates interstitial syndrome (thickened interlobular septa, subpleural edema from pulmonary edema, ARDS, or interstitial lung disease).



Q2. Lung sliding is absent on the left after intubation. How do you distinguish right mainstem intubation from left pneumothorax?






Caution





Answer Clinical context first: just intubated → mainstem intubation is far more likely. Withdraw the ETT and reassess — if left sliding returns, it was mainstem intubation. For pneumothorax: find a lung point (the transition from absent to present sliding) — if present, pneumothorax is confirmed. Also, lung pulse (cardiac pulsations transmitted through apneic lung) may be visible in mainstem intubation but absent in pneumothorax. B-lines anywhere on the left rule out pneumothorax at that location.



Q3. What is the PLAPS point, and why is it the highest-yield location in a supine patient?






Caution





Answer The PLAPS (posterior lateral alveolar and/or pleural syndrome) point is at the lateral chest wall, at the level of the lower BLUE point, extended posteriorly. In a supine patient, both pleural fluid and consolidation accumulate in the most dependent (posterior) zones. The PLAPS point captures this dependent region without requiring the patient to sit up or roll over.



Q4. You see consolidation with dynamic air bronchograms in the right lower lobe. What does this tell you, and how does it differ from static air bronchograms?






Caution





Answer Dynamic air bronchograms (moving with respiration) indicate that the consolidated segment is still being ventilated — the airways are patent and air is moving in and out. This pattern is highly consistent with pneumonia. Static (fixed) air bronchograms suggest the airways are not patent — either the lobe is completely consolidated (massive pneumonia) or there is an obstructive process (mucus plug, foreign body, endobronchial tumor) causing collapse. Static bronchograms should prompt bronchoscopy consideration.



Q5. A patient with acute dyspnea has bilateral anterior A-lines and lung sliding. The BLUE protocol sends you to check for DVT. Why?






Caution





Answer Bilateral anterior A-lines with lung sliding means the anterior lung fields are normally aerated — ruling out cardiogenic pulmonary edema (which would show B-lines) and pneumothorax (which would show absent sliding). In the BLUE protocol, this pattern combined with DVT on compression ultrasound has an 81% positive predictive value for pulmonary embolism as the cause of respiratory failure — the lung fields are clear because the problem is vascular, not alveolar.

title: Module 10 — DVT Compression Ultrasound
text:
What clinical question does this exam answer, and how do findings change management?






Note



The bedside decision frame: One question with direct treatment implications.
Is there a proximal deep vein thrombosis?
A non-compressible deep vein = DVT until proven otherwise. In the right clinical context — unexplained hypoxia, tachycardia, submassive or massive PE — identifying a proximal DVT confirms the diagnosis of venous thromboembolism and supports anticoagulation or escalated therapy. In an ICU patient with unilateral leg swelling or a femoral catheter, DVT changes the catheter management plan and informs decisions about therapeutic anticoagulation vs prophylaxis.


Bedside DVT compression ultrasound (CUS) is a point-of-care test for proximal lower extremity DVT. The principle is simple: a normal vein fully collapses under probe pressure; a thrombosed vein does not. Two-point compression (common femoral vein and popliteal vein) is the standard for bedside providers. Three-zone compression (adding the femoral vein in the thigh) increases sensitivity for thigh DVT.

title: Module 10 — DVT Compression Ultrasound
text:
2. Image acquisition
Probe, windows, and technique for this module.
Use a high-frequency linear probe (7–15 MHz) — the veins are superficial and require resolution rather than penetration. Place the machine on the vascular preset.
Patient positioning: - Femoral vein: supine, leg slightly externally rotated and abducted (“frog leg” position) - Popliteal vein: patient in lateral decubitus (affected leg on top) or prone, or supine with the knee flexed over a rolled towel


Common femoral vein






Tip



Video slot: CFV acquisition — femoral triangle anatomy, compression technique, distinguishing vein from artery.


Probe placement: Transverse plane, in the femoral triangle, just below the inguinal ligament. The common femoral artery and vein appear side by side. The vein is medial, larger, and more compressible. Color Doppler shows phasic venous flow in the vein.
Compression technique: Apply firm, steady downward pressure on the probe until the vein walls touch. A normal vein fully collapses — walls coapt completely with moderate pressure. Scan from the inguinal ligament distally to the femoral bifurcation (into the superficial femoral and deep femoral veins). Compress every 1–2 cm.
Key landmark: The saphenofemoral junction (where the great saphenous vein enters the common femoral vein) must be identified and included — isolated saphenous thrombus has different treatment implications than CFV thrombosis.



Femoral vein (thigh)






Tip



Video slot: Femoral vein in the thigh — superficial femoral vein (misnomer: it is a deep vein), compression at mid-thigh.


Probe placement: Continue distally from the CFV, following the femoral (superficial femoral) vein through the thigh to Hunter’s canal. This portion is sometimes called the “superficial femoral vein” — a misnomer that has caused undertreatment, because it is actually a deep vein and DVT here carries the same PE risk as proximal DVT.



Popliteal vein






Tip



Video slot: Popliteal fossa acquisition — popliteal vein posterior to the artery, compression technique in the knee-flexed position.


Probe placement: Popliteal fossa, transverse plane. The popliteal artery is deep (anterior on the image) and the popliteal vein is superficial (posterior on the image). Compress from the popliteal crease proximally to where the vein bifurcates into the calf veins (tibial and peroneal). Calf DVT is not routinely assessed in basic two-point CUS.

title: Module 10 — DVT Compression Ultrasound
text:
3. Normal & normal variants






Tip



Video slots: Normal two-point compression — CFV and popliteal vein fully compressing to zero diameter. Color Doppler augmentation. Spontaneous phasic venous flow.



Normal compressibility
A normal vein walls coapt completely with gentle-to-moderate probe pressure. There should be no residual lumen. If the vein does not fully compress, this is abnormal until proven otherwise.


Normal venous Doppler

Phasic flow: Venous flow increases with expiration and decreases or stops with inspiration (opposite of arterial flow). This phasicity reflects transmitted respiratory pressure changes.
Augmentation: Distal compression of the calf (squeeze the calf) should produce a brisk increase in flow at the popliteal and femoral veins. Absent augmentation suggests obstruction between the compression point and the probe.
Spontaneous flow: Large proximal veins should show spontaneous flow on color Doppler without augmentation. Absence of spontaneous flow suggests elevated venous pressure or obstruction.



Differentiating vein from artery

title: Module 10 — DVT Compression Ultrasound
text:
4. Pathology library
Organized by finding.

Non-compressible vein — acute DVT






Tip



Video slots: - Non-compressible CFV — vein fails to collapse with firm probe pressure - Echogenic thrombus within the vein lumen - Anechoic (fresh) thrombus — non-compressible but nearly invisible without compression


A vein that does not fully collapse under firm probe pressure contains thrombus. The diagnosis of DVT requires non-compressibility — not the visual appearance of thrombus in the lumen.
Thrombus echogenicity:

Anechoic (echo-free): Fresh thrombus (hours to days old). The lumen appears nearly normal on 2D — non-compressibility is the only finding. This is a critical trap: an anechoic lumen that does not compress is still a DVT.
Hypoechoic: Subacute thrombus.
Echogenic/heterogeneous: Older, organizing thrombus. May be partially adherent to the wall.

Extent of thrombosis:

Proximal DVT: CFV, femoral vein, or popliteal vein — high PE risk, requires therapeutic anticoagulation.
Isolated distal (calf) DVT: Below the popliteal trifurcation — lower PE risk. Management is debated (serial surveillance vs anticoagulation based on symptoms and risk factors). Not routinely detected on two-point CUS.

Teaching points:

Always compress — do not rely on thrombus visualization. Fresh thrombus is anechoic and invisible on 2D imaging.
Proximal DVT = therapeutic anticoagulation in the absence of contraindications.
Catheter-associated DVT (from a femoral central venous catheter) requires catheter removal and anticoagulation — same risk as spontaneous DVT.
DVT in the context of unexplained hemodynamic instability should prompt cardiac echo for RV strain (see BLUE protocol, Module 8).




Partial compressibility






Tip



Video slot: Partial non-compressibility — vein compressed but not fully coaptated, residual lumen visible.


Partial non-compressibility indicates thrombus that does not fully occlude the vein. The vein compresses but a residual lumen remains visible.
Teaching points:

Any residual lumen on compression = positive study.
Do not confuse partial compression from inadequate probe pressure with partial non-compressibility from thrombus. Apply firm pressure — if in doubt, press harder.
Partial or non-occlusive thrombus carries the same PE risk as occlusive thrombus and requires the same anticoagulation.




Absent augmentation






Tip



Video slot: Absent augmentation — calf compression fails to increase flow at the femoral level.


When distal compression produces no augmentation of proximal flow, there is obstruction between the compression point and the probe. This suggests DVT between the two locations.
Teaching points:

Absent augmentation at the popliteal level with calf compression suggests popliteal or femoral DVT.
Absent augmentation at the CFV with thigh compression suggests femoral DVT.
Use augmentation to extend the reach of your assessment when visualization is limited.




Mimics and pitfalls







Mimic
Distinguishing Feature




Baker’s cyst
Posterior knee, anechoic cystic structure, posterior to the vein, fully compressible


Lymph node
Echogenic center (hilum), oval shape, not in the vein lumen


Superficial thrombophlebitis
Superficial vein (great saphenous), not the deep vein


Inguinal lymphadenopathy
Adjacent to but separate from the CFV, oval, does not compress within the vein


Hematoma
Adjacent, does not follow the vein, no flow on Doppler


Femoral vein valve
Normal valve leaflets may appear echogenic — they move with flow and do not cause non-compressibility

title: Module 10 — DVT Compression Ultrasound
text:
5. Integration cases
Cases where the finding changes management.


Case 1: Submassive PE — confirming the diagnosis
Clinical scenario: A 52-year-old woman presents with 3 days of dyspnea and right-sided pleuritic chest pain. HR 108, O2 sat 93% on room air. D-dimer 8,400 ng/mL. CT is pending (60-minute wait). Bedside echo shows mild RV dilation.
What exam would you perform? Two-point DVT compression ultrasound while CT is being arranged.






Tip



Video slot: Loops for interpretation.


What you see: Right CFV: non-compressible. Echogenic thrombus visible in the lumen. Right popliteal vein: fully compressible. Left: fully compressible bilaterally.
How does this change management? Right proximal DVT in a patient with dyspnea, tachycardia, pleuritic chest pain, elevated D-dimer, and RV dilation on echo. This is sufficient to diagnose VTE and begin anticoagulation without waiting for CT. Start therapeutic anticoagulation now. CT, when available, will characterize the pulmonary clot burden and guide risk stratification for advanced therapy. The DVT exam has compressed the time to anticoagulation.



Case 2: ICU patient with unilateral leg swelling
Clinical scenario: A 68-year-old man is day 10 in the ICU following abdominal surgery for perforated diverticulitis. He develops left leg swelling and pain. He has been on DVT prophylaxis with enoxaparin 40 mg daily. He is not anticoagulated therapeutically.
What exam would you perform? Left lower extremity DVT compression ultrasound.






Tip



Video slot: Loops for interpretation.


What you see: Left CFV: non-compressible, homogeneous hypoechoic thrombus. Left femoral vein: non-compressible through the thigh. Left popliteal vein: non-compressible.
How does this change management? Proximal DVT extending from CFV to popliteal vein despite prophylaxis. Transition to therapeutic anticoagulation (weight-based LMWH or unfractionated heparin depending on renal function and bleeding risk). Assess the bleeding risk in the context of his recent abdominal surgery — if high risk, consider IVC filter as a bridge. Hematology or vascular surgery consultation is appropriate for extensive proximal DVT.



Case 3: DVT evaluation after femoral catheter removal
Clinical scenario: A 55-year-old woman had a right femoral arterial line and a right femoral venous catheter in place for 10 days. Both were removed yesterday. Today she reports right groin pain and fullness.
What exam would you perform? Right femoral DVT compression ultrasound.






Tip



Video slot: Loops for interpretation.


What you see: Right CFV: partially non-compressible. Small residual lumen visible under firm compression. Echogenic thrombus along the posterior wall. No color flow in the occluded segment. Right femoral vein in thigh: fully compressible.
How does this change management? Catheter-associated DVT of the right CFV. Therapeutic anticoagulation for a minimum of 3 months (or for the duration of any ongoing catheter risk factor). Remove any remaining venous access from the affected limb if possible. DVT in a catheter site that extends to the CFV carries PE risk equivalent to spontaneous DVT.






Tip



Case format reminder: The case ends with a management decision, not just a diagnosis.

Quiz

Note



Q1. The vein appears anechoic (echo-free) on 2D imaging but does not fully compress. Is this a DVT?






Caution





Answer Yes. Fresh (acute) thrombus is anechoic and nearly invisible on 2D imaging. Non-compressibility is the diagnostic criterion for DVT — not visual detection of thrombus in the lumen. A vein that fails to fully collapse under firm probe pressure contains thrombus, regardless of its 2D echogenicity. This is the most important concept in DVT compression ultrasound.



Q2. The popliteal vein compresses normally but there is no augmentation of popliteal flow with calf compression. What does this suggest?






Caution





Answer Absent augmentation indicates obstruction between the compression point (calf) and the probe position (popliteal fossa). This suggests DVT in the calf veins (tibial or peroneal) that is not detected by compression at the popliteal level. Extended assessment of the calf veins or serial surveillance ultrasound in 5–7 days is appropriate if clinical suspicion remains high.



Q3. The “superficial femoral vein” is non-compressible on compression ultrasound. A colleague says this is not a proximal DVT because it is “superficial.” How do you respond?






Caution





Answer The superficial femoral vein is a deep vein despite its misleading name — it is part of the deep venous system and DVT at this level carries the same PE risk as common femoral or popliteal DVT. The term “superficial” refers to its relative position within the thigh (as opposed to the deep femoral vein), not to its anatomic classification as superficial vs deep. This misnomer has historically led to undertreatment.



Q4. How does DVT compression ultrasound integrate with the BLUE protocol for diagnosing PE?






Caution





Answer In the BLUE protocol, when bilateral anterior lung zones show A-lines and lung sliding (ruling out pulmonary edema and pneumothorax), the next step is DVT compression ultrasound. The presence of DVT in this context has an 81% positive predictive value for PE as the cause of respiratory failure. A positive DVT exam + abnormal RV on cardiac echo is sufficient evidence to initiate anticoagulation for suspected PE without CT in an unstable patient.



Q5. What is the clinical significance of a Baker’s cyst in the popliteal fossa, and how do you distinguish it from popliteal DVT?






Caution





Answer A Baker’s cyst (popliteal cyst) is a synovial fluid collection that can rupture and cause calf pain and swelling mimicking DVT. On ultrasound, it appears as an anechoic cystic structure in the popliteal fossa, medial and posterior to the joint, separate from the popliteal vein. Key distinguishing features: the Baker’s cyst does not lie within the vein lumen, the popliteal vein adjacent to it is fully compressible, and there is no intraluminal thrombus. A ruptured Baker’s cyst may track distally with irregular margins.
